Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to raise a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That this House expresses its strong condemnation of the government's decision announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and contemptuously of parliament in that it was made outside the House, of the recognition by Canada of the Palestine Liberation Organization, which cannot but be harmful to the State of Israel and to world peace, it having been made clear by the Prime Minister of Israel last Thursday that Israel will not negotiate with the Palestine Liberation Organization, as he said: 'its prime aim is to strangle the Jewish state. They want the destruction of the State of Israel. It is the essence of their philosophy and policy.'

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue and is in respect of a question raised a week ago concerning a dangerous precedent which had been established by officials regarding the possible change in the tax exemption status of charitable organizations. speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN ACTIVITIES OF ORGANIZATIONS
subsubtopic: DESIGNATED CHARITABLE ORGANIZATIONS UNDER ACT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Interestingly enough, but maybe not surprising, "charitable purpose" is not defined in the act so we had to turn to the courts for an interpretation. They have indicated that "for charitable purposes" includes relief of poverty, advancement of religion, advancement of education and an obscure clause, of general benefit to the community. So, first and foremost, when we are defining what charitable activity is we must look to those engaged in other activities. "Political activity" again has no definition in the act. It has been indicated in the courts that "engaged in political activity", is an adjunct to political activity and does in fact void the charitable aspect. We in the department have no wish to be unduly restrictive. In point of fact, the department has taken the position that presenting a viewpoint does not in fact void the charitable status. This is an area where I do back up my officials. They had to depend on the only precedent they had in this particular instance, that is the jurisprudence of the land, and because of that, and the difficulties this might make for many organizations, I am asking my officials to look at it in more depth.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JUSTICE MINISTER HAIM ZADOK OF ISRAEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. While I have no objection to going through the exercise of standing to be recognized-and I recognize the fact that there are many other hon. members who must be recognized-I should like to point out one fact which disturbed me last Friday and today. Conveniently or otherwise, ministers who could have been questioned have had occasion to leave the House during the question period. I noticed that after the question put by the hon. member for Central Nova to the Minister of Labour there was consultation between the Minister of Labour and the Solicitor General. I do not say that consultation was pertinent, but I noticed that immediately afterwards the Solicitor General left the House. I also noticed that the minister's parliamentary secretary enjoyed his peregrinations behind the curtain for the entire balance of the question period. I find it indeed frustrating, as must other hon. members, to be recognized when ministers and their parliamentary secretaries do not sit regularly in the House.
It should be noted that some ministers and some parliamentary secretaries are very faithful to the question period and recognize the urgency of the need for hon. members to determine what the facts are, but there are some who very seriously abuse the purpose of the question period. As a backbencher, I simply want to voice my serious objection to this abuse of the question period by both ministers and parliamentary secretaries. Quite frankly, I am fed up.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its lack of an industrial strategy which (a) has resulted in falling production, job losses and uncertainty, as in the cases of Westinghouse, Microsystems, Dunlop Tire and others, and (b) is a major cause of today's unemployment rate of 7.4 per cent, which means that 761,000 Canadians are without jobs, a situation that calls for immediate action.
He said: Mr. Speaker, our purpose in bringing this motion to the attention of the House is to indicate what we think is probably the most important cause of unemployment in Canada, that is, the lack of an industrial strategy on the part of the government, to try to make some specific references and to draw some lessons from those references as to why we have failed to create jobs in this country. It takes some kind of perverse genius for a government to create a disaster in a land as fortunate as Canada, with all its resources both human and material.
The people on the other side of the House must have to try very hard to give us probably the highest level of unemployment in the western world, a rate of 7.4 per cent: they really have to work at it. It is not that the problem of an industrial strategy and its effect on unemployment has not been studied in this country. If we are good at anything at all, it is studying things. While we may not have much of a military strategy, we certainly have a "navel" policy in the sense that we keep looking at our own all the
Industrial Strategy
time. However, nothing seems to do much good. We have had all these studies going back to the royal commission of Walter Gordon. It seems hardly a year goes by that something is not studied. Occasionally work is found for the other place, and its members throw in a study. We have set national objectives. It is not as if we do not know what sort of policies we want to have.
We started off with the objectives of the Economic Council of Canada for an industrial and economic approach. We went on to the approach of the Science Council. Then a number of years ago the government brought out a foreign policy review paper which was supposed to set down the kinds of objectives this country wanted to achieve in terms of social and economic policy. If we go back even further than that, we find that a man who was not very prone to do any planning at all had his own kind of review policy. Following the Second World War, Mackenzie King in fact had a study commissioned to see what we could come up with in terms of a strategy.
We do not need to do any more studying. There are studies all around us. What we need is a government which is determined to do something from what has been studied until now. I can appreciate that planning is not an easy thing to do, that there are difficulties in a country like Canada, and that there are differences between provinces and differences between various groups in our society which have to be reconciled.
Of course, it is very easy for a government to simply ignore the problem and take the attitude that if they do nothing about it, perhaps it will go away. For years and years they were able to live off the resources of this country, not doing anything, and the problem tended, if not to go away at least to go underground. We are reaching a new stage in our development, however, where that is not going to be so easy. We are no longer as rich as we were. We can no longer count on the bounty of nature, the oil under the ground or the minerals that were easy to obtain, in order to be assured of our future. We will have to start thinking about where we are going and about conserving our resources. While the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talks about a new society, there is no evidence that his government has dealt with the old society, let alone know what they are going to do with the new one.
To demonstrate some of the points I wish to make, perhaps we should look at what might be called a Tale of two Cities. One is the city of Hamilton, and the other the city of Whitby. One has to do with appliances, and the other with tires. Their experiences demonstrate why we have not been able to create enough jobs in Canada, and the shortsightedness of our government in developing strategy. Recently, the leader of my party received a letter from Mr. William Love, president of local 494 of the United Rubber Workers Union, in which he expressed concern about what has been happening in the Whitby plant that was bought from Dunlop by Firestone.
Briefly, the history of the plant shows that it was formerly owned by Dunlop Canada Limited and was sold to Firestone Tire Company in August, 1974, when it was given the name Whitby Tire Limited. Since October, 1975, the name has been changed to Dayton Tire Canada Lim-

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
ited. That company has laid off approximately 120 employees indefinitely and has lost another 70 employees due to those who quit or retired and have not been replaced. There had been 530 members of the bargaining unit under Dunlop, and when Firestone bought the plant they promised to increased employment by 200 or 300 people. Production at the plant has dropped from an average of 6,000 passenger and truck tires per day to the present level of 3,000 tires per day. There does not seem to be any plan to increase production above 3,000 tires a day for the balance of the year, and the union is worried that there will be further lay-offs.
I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) if he would look into conditions at this company. Firestone can no longer use the "Dunlop" name because there was a three-year agreement that they would manufacture tires under the Dunlop licence and then start to manufacture an unbranded line. Dunlop was going to continue production of tires, but in the United States where they could take advantage of the "Dunlop" trade name. They would then sell the tires to Canada. We received information that Dunlop were setting up warehouses, or encouraging distributorships by assuring them that there would be tires of every size and line shipped to them from the United States.
When we approach the government and point out that jobs are being lost in this country, they generally reply that it is because of a soft market in the United States. They always give that reason, instead of the reason being their own soft heads. In this case, however, we are talking about the Canadian market. What happened was very convenient for Dunlop. There was a great fuss three years ago when Dunlop closed down operations in Canada, but it was pointed out that Firestone was taking over and production in this country would continue. But it seems, now, that Firestone used that time to organize the transfer of production from Canada to the United States.
The rubber industry is an example of one of the things that is wrong with this country's industrial organization. Because of a foreign ownership pattern of setting up branch plants in Canada, we have a miniature replica of the American market, and to some extent the British market. Every major brand name is represented in Canada. If one is missed, the government goes out and encourages a French manufacturer to come in.
It does not take much knowledge or business to see that if we cannot handle the number of brands and options we already have in a market one-eleventh the size of the United States market, that it is impossible for us to get the long runs necessary for the efficient production we need to allow us to compete. That, coupled with the fact that some of these companies set up plants, then go back to the United States and export to Canada, cuts our market into pieces. The government talks about plans to step up exports and invade other markets; but, Mr. Speaker, before we can take other markets we must be able to look after our own. In many instances we have failed to satisfy our own market, and therefore we have a weak industry.
A radio interviewer spoke to me this afternoon before I came into the chamber. He wanted to know whether I intended to talk about productivity. I told him that was not the main theme of my discourse and I would speak about it

only indirectly. He asked if worker productivity is the problem. I replied that when people talk about productivity they assume it is directly related to the worker. Mr. Speaker, a worker can only be as productive as is permitted by the industrial structure in which he works; he depends on the tools and machinery that are supplied. He cannot produce tires just by sweating; he needs technical organization, marketing expertise and, in general, a rational industry-which this industry is not.
Studies show that this country employs more capital per worker than any other, including the United States, yet our workers are not as productive. That is not because they do not work as hard; it is because industry is organized in such a way as to make it virtually impossible to get high productivity in this country while providing the number of jobs needed. When workers in this country ask for parity of wages with their counterparts in the United States because they claim they work as hard, the companies tell them that they are only interested in cheap labour in Canada and do not wish to give them parity because it will price them out of foreign markets. When the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) speaks he will give some examples of this from his own riding.
I remember when there was a strike at Massey-Ferguson, in the Brantford area, and a consultant was hired by the company to explain to the workers why they could not receive parity with American workers. The argument he put forward was that the company had concentrated its labour-intensive production in Canada, and if they had to pay the same wages here as in the United States they might as well move to the United States. That was not a foreign company, Mr. Speaker, but a Canadian company.
What had happened to the free trade that was supposed to be the panacea to all Canada's industrial problems was that a great Canadian company transferred all its high technology to the United States. Its capital-intensive production was concentrated there, and it left little more than assembly-line plants in Canada. In effect, it was telling workers in Canada that if they wanted even this kind of employment, they would have to accept a lower standard of living than their counterparts in the United States. That kind of argument could hardly be accepted by the workers.
I have spoken about Dunlop and what happened there. The work was transferred to Firestone, because Dunlop has the name, can export to Canada, does not need a plant in this country, has built up consumer confidence in its name and has used the deductibility of advertising, which should have been a capital consideration rather than a deductible one, to enhance its position. Now the employment will take place in another country, but the market will be in Canada.
In Hamilton, the same situation faces us. In that city an industry producing white goods, Westinghouse, is up for sale. A Canadian manufacturer, GSW, wants to buy this industry. They thought a sale would take place and that the name "Westinghouse" would go with the sale. To their surprise, the parent of Westinghouse said, "No, you have no right to the name and cannot use it in the white goods industry." The Canadian company said that if they could not use the name or make some arrangement to use the
May 17, 1976

Westinghouse name, the American company could simply move in with exports from the United States which would compete with the product of the Canadian company, products manufactured by the assets the Canadian company had acquired.
What has happened? FIRA has turned down the American application to buy out Westinghouse. Presumably, it has not said anything about the Canadian application, because the Canadian application is not before FIRA and FIRA does not have to rule on a take-over by a Canadian company. There seems to be a fair amount of sympathy on the part of FIRA for the Canadian company to take over Westinghouse. The recommendation has gone to cabinet.
It seems, from all we hear that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is sympathetic to the recommendation of FIRA. But this has been going on since last August and there has been no decision from cabinet on the matter. We have heard complaints from the Canadian company, GSW, which is a reputable company. It says it thought it understood what the Canadian government wanted; it thought it understood Canadian industrial strategy, which was aimed at rationalizing the white goods industry. At one time there were as many manufacturers of refrigerators in Canada as in the United States-an impossible situation. The company thought that the government intended to rationalize industry. Although this government has never had an industrial strategy, it has brought in sectoral policies which deal with one industry or another.
At any rate, GSW was under the impression that the Canadian government had such a policy and would welcome a Canadian company taking over a foreign company in Canada for the purpose of rationalizing. Their position seemed strong. It was reinforced by the union which wrote to the Canadian government and said, "We prefer the GSW take-over rather than the White Industries' take-over." They recognized that White Industries have not been a positive influence. White Industries were in London; they closed the plant down as soon as they bought another. Their attitude to labour-management relations leaves much to be desired. So you have the unions supporting the GSW company. On top of that, the Committee for an Independent Canada also supported the GSW take-over. Therefore, FIRA was against the American take-over; there has been positive support for the Canadian company, but the matter has been in abeyance before cabinet since last August. Why?
I will tell you one reason, Mr. Speaker. The government is afraid of the United States, afraid to make this kind of decision and afraid of being accused of favouring a Canadian company. I wonder why that is the government's attitude in matters of industrial strategy, matters which involve the jobs of people and the future livelihood of this country. Why is the government so afraid? Evidently there was no such fear in the case of Time magazine-although there was at one "time". Excuse the pun. But the government changed its attitude. It is hard to know why the government has not made a decision on this amalgamation or take-over, whichever way you want to look at it.
It seems to me that it is vital to establish a strong Canadian industry, whether publicly or privately-owned. In our view, we need a strong Canadian industry. It seems
Industrial Strategy
to me that the cabinet should have made its decision a long time ago. Failing that, it should at least make its decision now. That decision should be in favour of GSW, the Canadian company, rather than in favour of an American company.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) does not mind, before I sit down I will be happy to accept his question. The question of trademarks is involved in this matter. I must underline the importance of trademarks as they are a factor which make it virtually impossible for Canadians to compete. There are many weaknesses among Canadian capitalists. On the other hand, the Canadian capitalist who must compete with the American giant and the advantages of American capitalists faces many difficulties.
In the case of Dunlop, how does one compete? Firestone sets up a plant which will produce unbranded lines. Dunlop has the name, has set up its distributorship system and can take advantage of overflow advertising. This has been going on over the years. Tires are a bit of a mystery to most people. The government has not adopted any adequate way whereby the public can be told, "This is a good tire. That is a bad tire." There is no comparative testing, and tires need not conform to any standards except the manufacturing standards. Therefore, the consumer is placed in the position of not knowing and must depend on the brand name. When you have a brand name, you have a stranglehold on a particular market. The point is that all the brand names in this country are American brand names, and as long as American firms can use those brand names in Canada they have a stranglehold on the Canadian market unless we break it.
I have had discussions over the years with members of the government who have said that perhaps we should act unilaterally in the case of Westinghouse and do something about the brand name. What they do not see is that it would be wrong to do this with one specific company. By
13572

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
doing this you would be arbitrary and discriminatory and the government might have a tough time if it were taken to court. No government, particularly a Canadian government, has the right to behave in that way. If it wants to bring in a policy, it must apply it to everybody. It must have a general policy on brand names. Brand names are becoming a problem-a problem concerning FIRA in cases of the Canadian take-over of American industries. This is probably the most serious impediment to rationalizing the Canadian industry and the ability of Canadians to take over American industries, and the government must do something about it. They say, "No other country has disallowed brand names or the use of brand names."

speechtext: No other country has the same degree of foreign ownership of its industries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
No other country has the same degree of foreign ownership of its industries. It is no good behaving like Boy Scouts. Boy Scouts are well and good, but not when you are involved in these kinds of enterprises. We are living next to the United States and they have a stranglehold on our economy. I do not blame the Americans for anything; I have never blamed the Americans. The only person you should blame for being stupid is yourself. This government and governments before it have been stupid in permitting the degree of foreign ownership which has grown up in this country. They must do something about that now. I know that there are cabinet committees trying to deal with this business of trademarks. They will have to find a way whereby if a Canadian industry or company takes over a foreign industry or company, the use of certain foreign trademarks used by the company in this country will be a matter of national interest. We are the only country in the world with this problem.
I know that there are international conventions on trademarks and that suggestions in this field are not to be made lightly. Some of these matters are settled in international agreements, and I am generally in favour of international agreements. But when something this big is involved, when we are concerned about what has happened in the country because of historical developments, I think the rest of the world will understand if we act. We are not trying to take anything away; we are not trying to take any right away; we merely wish to say that certain trademarks will not be allowed to be used in this country.
I have said that the use of manufacturers' brand advertising and trade marks is, in many cases, one of the reasons we cannot reduce costs and achieve more effective production units. Even if we in Canada wanted to limit selling costs-and it has been proposed that we should limit them as a deductible item-there is too much huckstering going on; it would not do much good. This is pointed out by Canadian advertisers. All you would do is ensure an even larger share of the Canadian market to the Americans because their overflow advertising dominates this country. Every attempt at national policy would be frustrated in this area because we have permitted them to take advantage of a name that has been built up in another country. There was a time when trade marks and brand names provided important reassurance to the consumer about

quality. That was a time when butchers had heavy fingers, scales were not weighted, crackers came in big barrels and were not packaged-but that day has passed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Look at Ford.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Yes, even the trade mark is no longer a guarantee of quality. The public, of course, needs some kind of reassurance. They need something better, in the way of reassurance, than brand names. Why should not gasoline be sold by octane rating or some other definable quality, in the same way meat is sold by definable quality, rather than by brand? There would be much better assurance to the consumer. It would certainly be much less costly in terms of advertising.
We see now that there is a growth of unbranded lines in Canada. People are in fact moving to reliable dealers and substituting confidence in the retailer for confidence in the brand name. That sort of thing should be helped along. There is some question that FIRA has the power to deal with brand names. That is not at all certain. If FIRA does not have power, it should be given it. I have watched the activities of FIRA. I know there has been a lot of criticism of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. Some think they are doing too much, and others not enough. I have come to the conclusion that they are trying very hard to do a job.
In some cases, FIRA is usurping the authority that properly belongs to the politician. In the committee hearing the other day I asked the vice-president of FIRA whether he found the absence of an industrial strategy was creating difficulties for himself in terms of trying to make decisions about what was of advantage to Canada. With a little laugh he said, "Well, we make it up as we go along", or words to that effect. He was not going to comment on whether it was an industrial strategy. Because there is not political decision of industrial strategy, and because there has been no intelligent sitting down and determining what should be our strategy in Canada, agencies like FIRA are making decisions. I am not going to condemn FIRA for making that decision, because somebody has to do something, but surely it is wrong for policy to come in by this back door way.
I hear members of the government criticize the bureaucracy, the civil service, for usurping power unto themselves. When that happens in the civil services it is because the political leaders have failed to make the decisions even though they clearly have that power. Decisions are going to be made. If they are not made by the elected representatives of the people, they will be made by the captains of industry or the bureaucrats. Somebody will come to some conclusion. The proper people to do it are the representatives of the people, and the logical place for decisions to be made is here in the House of Commons. Members of parliament can be judged. If people approve of the decisions we make, we return: if not, they elect those who will make decisions of which they do approve.
My time is drawing to a close. There are a great many things to be said in this area. I have only touched very briefly on the problem. There is a question I would like to receive. This is a serious matter in terms of an industrial strategy. The government can now start, at least in a small way, to worry about employment in this country by seeing
May 17, 1976

that the GSW take-over is approved and by strengthening the hand of FIRA to deal with industrial property, as well as planning with regard to the state of economy and how to create more employment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to start by apologizing on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), for whom I am pinch-hitting. He had to honour a long-standing and significant commitment he had made in the west. I want to convey to the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) the minister's personal regret at not being present for the debate, and assure him that the comments made will be passed on to him in detail.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge covered a number of specifics and also generalized in the whole area of industrial strategy. While I will not be able to deal with many of the specifics in terms of local issues or particular cases, I want to spend a little time trying to get into focus the kind of industrialized performance of this country to which we are addressing ourselves when we talk about the need for an industrial strategy of some comprehensive nature. Before I do that, I want to point out that in the case of the White and GSW issue, this matter has not been neglected nor cavalierly treated. As the hon. member well knows, it involves some very complex issues, particularly the issue of trademarks.
There has been a great deal of consideration about it. I think the hon. member implied in his comments-in a quiet way, anyway-his recognition that there is a potential breach of a long-standing arrangement and the honouring of trademarking internationally. He also suggested that he recognized this could not be treated lightly when making a decision. Of course, that is at the very root of the GSW-White-Westinghouse dilemma.
Getting back to the more generalized approach, before we try and get at what an industrial strategy should or
Industrial Strategy
should not be we should get our sights clear on where we stand now with regard to performance in Canada. During the early 1970s the industrialized world experienced a boom of unprecedented proportions which led to a number of structural maladjustments and distortions-rapid and large changes in energy prices, food shortages, and other supply-demand imbalances. With this situation, economic adjustment and consolidation became inevitable.
The recession of 1974-75-and this is something I believe we often lose sight of-has been a worldwide phenomenon not peculiar to Canada, and although we may score points by emphasizing our own problems here, policy responses cannot be made in isolation. Unemployment rates and unused productive capacity in the major industrialized nations rose during the first half of 1975 to levels unprecedented since the end of the Second World War. For OECD countries combined, the real growth in the national product declined at a rate of about 5 per cent during the first half of the year. After that, economic conditions began to pick up.
The figures show that in comparison to other major industrialized countries, and with the OECD group in particular, Canada did not perform too badly. It experienced, during that period, a positive growth. The actual figure is .2 per cent, which is not one we would ordinarily boast about, but the fact is that every other country, with the exception of Japan, did worse. In the United States, it declined by 3 per cent; in France, it declined by 2 per cent; in Germany, by 3.5 per cent; and in Italy, by 4.5 per cent. As I say, Japan was the only other country within OECD to show positive growth, with an increase of 1.5 per cent. So we did not do so badly there.
In other words, the slackening of economic activity in Canada was much less severe than in most other nations. This is particularly true in comparison with the United States. We use such a comparison very often because, after all, the U.S. is our major market; it is close to us and there is a general similarity in our approaches to industry. Our real growth in 1975 was 3 per cent higher than in 1973, as against a decline of 4 per cent in the United States during the same period. The volume of industrial production in Canada declined by about 2 per cent between 1973 and 1975 but, again, one must compare this experience with a drop of over 9 per cent in the United States. The average unemployment rate in Canada for the three-year period was 5.9 per cent of the labour force, compared with 6.3 per cent in the United States.
More encouraging still, Mr. Speaker, economic activity in Canada has been advancing on a broadening front since the second quarter of last year. For example, output by industries which are producing goods was 3.2 per cent higher, on a seasonally adjusted basis, in January, 1976, than for the first quarter of 1975. Canadian employment in April, 1976, at 9.3 million, was 3 per cent above the total for the same month a year earlier. Exports for the first quarter of 1976 were 13 per cent higher than for the comparable period in 1975. Changes in export markets had been, in fact, the single most important factor in the slowdown of the Canadian economy.
95568-25%

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
The principal cause for the decline in the volume of goods exported in 1975 was the recession in the United States, our principal market, particularly in housing and automobiles, coupled with the modest level of recovery achieved in that country by the year-end. Another factor which contributed to the reduction in the volume of Canadian exports was the decline in the other OECD economies during the first half of the year and their sluggish recovery thereafter. These were circumstances which no strategy within Canada on a short-term basis could seriously affect.
Other factors include lower oil exports-made necessary for reasons which no doubt hon. members opposite understand-and based, really, on a shifting of policy rather than on market considerations. Our exports of pulp, paper and asbestos also suffered. One offsetting element came in the form of increased exports to OPEC countries. With the improvement in world economic activity now gaining strength, particularly in the United States, it is now our expectation that Canadian exports will expand and lead to a further strengthening of domestic economic activity.
Even though recorded unemployment for April, at 769,000, accounted for 7.4 per cent of the labour force, the Canadian experience in recent months has been better than in the United States. Moreover, it should be noted that the significance of any particular rate of unemployment is no longer the same in terms of economic hardship associated with a temporary loss of work, as was the case even five or ten years ago. Part of the reason for this is the substantial upgrading in the scale and extent of unemployment benefits.
Then, again, a much larger proportion of the unemployment total represents people who are in a position to change jobs, enter into or withdraw from the labour force at frequent intervals. Also of significance is the fact that despite an international recession, nearly 1V4 million more people were employed in Canada in 1975 than was the case at the start of this decade in 1970. This does represent a considerable achievement, given the fact that Canada has experienced the most rapid labour force growth among the industrialized countries of the world.
A great deal of attention is now being paid to Canada's productivity performance. The dominant factor in this area in 1974 and 1975 was the economic recession and, more recently, the beginning economic recovery. Statistics which purport to show that Canada's productivity performance in manufacturing has deteriorated are really only revealing the obvious, which is that favourable productivity depends in large measure on the stage of the business cycle. It is certainly true that during a business recession productivity is normally inferior because, in the face of a slackening in demand for durable goods which is reflected in industrial production, it is difficult to obtain good productivity performance in a situation where men and machines are underemployed and producing in well below optimum conditions. This is the stage at which Canada, along with nearly all the industrialized nations, found itself throughout most of 1974 and 1975.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, if we look at the facts we find that Canada's productivity in the manufacturing field has been relatively favourable. During the decade 1964-1974, output per man-hour increased by close to 4 per cent per year,

compared with an increase in the United States for the same period of only 3 per cent. We know that in 1975 our output per man-hour was virtually flat. On the other hand, in the United States it registered a decline of nearly 1 per cent.
In the initial stages of an economic slump, employers are loth immediately to lay off workers as demand declines, and this is reflected in relatively poor productivity. On the other hand, when the economy is coming out of a slump, then at least in the early stages of an uptrend large increases in output are registered, with very little increase in the work force. It is sad that in a way the growth of employment lags behind economic growth, but there is a gain in terms of productivity. I think it is important not to win debating points; rather, we should try to develop a proper policy response and should put these matters, in this case productivity, in their proper perspective. Productivity in both Canadian and United States' manufacturing should show a very marked improvement this year as the economic recovery gets well under way.
For several reasons, care should be taken in interpreting recent cyclical productivity changes and trends. First, statistical estimation has been unusually difficult because of rapid changes in the inflation rate. Unquestionably, these will be subject to later revision under the statistical base that we are using. Second, unusual changes have been taking place in the structure and use of the labour force, and these may have reduced the aggregate productivity trend in recent years. These changes include factors such as the increased use of part-time workers; particularly in this country, the sharp rise in the number of young people coming on to the labour market; and we are also attracting women into the market and seeing an increase in their participation rate. Finally, and regrettably, there was the relatively high level of strike activity in 1974 and 1975.
That gives the House the background to the situation, Mr. Speaker. Since we in this country tend to uncover, exploit, elaborate and dwell upon doom and gloom, I think it is also useful to look at some of the strengths of our economy, to put them all together in an attempt to reach some better policy response. We should not concentrate on overstressing gloom, or indulge in too much optimism about the good things; we should try to achieve a balance.
The government recognizes that continuing improvement in the levels of Canadian productivity is necessary and vital to enable the expectations of all our people to be fulfilled, as well as to ensure that Canadian industry remains relatively and competitively strong. Government policy has fairly consistently placed high priority on measures to sustain business investment in Canada, with particular emphasis on the manufacturing industry. Measures that were taken to achieve this aim have not always found favour with the opposition. I refer in particular to the budget measure of June, 1975, in regard to which the minister said this:
It is well known that our policies have sought to encourage a strong manufacturing sector. We have provided long-term tax incentives to assist our manufacturers and processors to compete in domestic and foreign markets.
May 17, 1976

So let hon. members not tell us that there has not been a strategy or a tactical approach. They might disagree and would put it another way, but that is a matter of program implementation, not necessarily policy disagreement. As I recall it, the then minister of finance went on to say that if our economy is to remain productive and competitive and capable of providing jobs, we must ensure that we have modern capital facilities with which to work and we must guard against any slowdown in investment. The budget of June, 1975, introduced an investment tax credit as a temporary extra incentive for investment in a wide range of new productive facilities. Hon. members will be familiar with the details.
Another element in the government's policy is to work, we hope increasingly closely and in more detail, with industry, provincial governments and labour. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has established a much more comprehensive consultative mechanism with industry to provide a systematic and structured framework for consultation. To date, seven industry sector consultative committees have been established, each of which is made up of a dozen or so executive officers of the industry who have been chosen as being able to make a positive and personal contribution to a better understanding by ourselves and industry of the performance of the particular sector concerned. These industry sector consultative committees are designed to act as a forum to review developments in industry, to ensure that the government is fully informed about matters affecting the health and viability of the particular industry, to identify emerging opportunities as well as clearly to establish constraints. This will enable us to have realistic policy and program development.
They are also designed to serve as a first-line sounding board for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and other federal departments against which tests may be made on industrial policy initiatives with either selective or across the board impact. They also have the objective of assisting in the identification of the need to develop specific sector policies and, as appropriate, to assist in the establishment of specific sector committees as well as to assist the government in communicating government policies to industry.
Committees are also in place for the chemicals, machinery, iron and steel, furniture and forestry products industries. In addition, five special sector committees have been established which will, on an ad hoc basis, provide advice and input on sector opportunities and constraints and options available to deal with them. More specifically, the special sector committees will assist the department in developing an in-depth analysis of the sector structure and performance in the domestic and international environment; in evaluating the current and future prospects for the sector, taking account of regional, national and international advantages and constraints. They will also identify the contribution that the industry can make to the national economy in terms of industrial development goals and outline the constraints that might inhibit achievement of these goals. They will propose policy initiatives which the government can take to assist industry in increasing its contribution to national objectives.
Industrial Strategy
These and other initiatives are in keeping with developments and are in addition to the ongoing consultation and discussion that takes place with industry and between federal and provincial governments at various levels. I think the record shows a consistent emphasis on measures to promote the development of an internationally competitive manufacturing and processing industry in Canada, with emphasis on improving our industrial efficiency.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I regret my colleague had to be away. He would very much have preferred to change his arrangements, but that was impossible. We will take note of all the points that are made by various speakers. The minister's parliamentary secretary is here as well, and between the two of us we will convey to the minister the constructive points that are made, and try to debate and answer those that might not, in our opinion, be so constructive.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate which has been introduced by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman). I should just like to make reference to what I think is the key word in his motion. The motion commences:
That this House condemns the government for its lack of an industrial strategy-
I think we should focus on the word "strategy"; certainly that particular word was missing in the response of the minister. In responding to the opening speech in this debate, the minister said that part of the difficulty we are in today is caused by world wide inflation. He excused the government on the ground that energy costs so much in Canada today. He went on to say that we only had a .2 per cent increase in the gross national product, and took some pride in the fact that Canada at least had some increase while many other nations showed a decrease. What we are missing in this whole position is recognition, by the tone of what the minister said, of the fact that there is no strategy within Canada relating to incentives to industry and industrial development in this country.
The minister went on to point out some projects the government is attempting to implement, such as the incentive investment tax credit. What this really means, when we think of the semantics of the word "strategy", is that we do not have an over-all approach but, rather, something that is growing like Topsy. We have the handling of one problem when it arises or surfaces in a crisis situation. Then the government opts to handle the next most important crisis as it comes along. I think this is unacceptable for a country such as Canada, with one of the greatest natural resource bases of any country in the world, a country with one of the greatest human resources and a country with very substantial energy resources. This country has energy resources far beyond its fossil fuels, oil and natural gas. We have energy resources in this country in the form of vast basins of hydrocarbons-and I mean our coal deposits. We also have a tremendous undeveloped source of energy in this country, and I think of water tidal power and wind power.
The suggestion that we are in the situation we are in at the present time because of the increase in the number of

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
women entering the work force is really an admission by the government that it is not prepared to cope with the situation. That kind of excuse is unacceptable from the government. What it really means is that this government has not paid full attention to the fact that it is not only considered a right, but a normal situation of life in the 1970s that there should be adequate jobs for females entering the labour market. It is an admission by the government that it is not prepared to gear up to the kind of society which allows full participation of both females and males in the work force of this nation.
The government talks about the sluggish market in the European Economic Community and the decrease in our exports of oil and other products. All I can suggest is that if we take that kind of approach for not being at the industrial level we ought to be at in this country, all we are really saying is that we are puppets of the international economy, being manipulated by forces outsides our own control. This, then, is a full admission that Canada as a nation does not have an industrial strategy. That is exactly what this motion is all about.
In listening to the response by the minister-which was a listing, cataloguing or a detailing of excuses the government has for the situation in which we find ourselves-it all added up to one simple conclusion, that is, that the motion is certainly accurate. Indeed, there is certainly no industrial strategy when one considers the meaning and the perspective of that word.
If we are talking about military strategy in time of war, we are talking about the whole effort in terms of strategy; how all the forces knit together in terms of attempting to reach an ultimate conclusion. The ultimate conclusion for Canada, in terms of industrial strategy, is the development of full employment. We did not hear, in the response by the minister, anything about what is to be included in the forthcoming budget, or anything about what is going to happen in 1976 and 1977 in the way of some new thrust or policy toward a strategy that in this country would lead to a position of full employment. This simply underscores the whole need for a motion such as the one put forward today. The motion simply points out, in fact, that in this nation there is no industrial strategy, and a full admission of that fact by the government today.
I should like to take some time to detail how serious is this lack of industrial strategy in our country today. The unemployment situation in April, 1976, was nothing less than atrocious. It has reached a level higher than any other since 1961; it went from 6.6 per cent in January of this year to 7.4 per cent in April. This means that since January until April of this year there were 80,000 more Canadians unemployed.
It is difficult to get a proper perspective of this unemployment situation and what it means to have 80,000 people unemployed. What it really means is that double the number on the voters' list in my constituency are now unemployed. I think this begins to point out the degree to which we have not addressed ourselves to providing full employment in this country, and how serious this fact is. Last year, between January and April, we had an increase in the number of unemployed of 65,000.
Another way of looking at the seriousness of unemployment and the damage it causes society is through a com-

parison of expenditures under the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Last year these expenditures increased by 90 per cent. When we consider this 90 per cent increase in expenditure through unemployment insurance, we must realize that this was in the first couple of months of the year when this nation had almost stable employment.
What has been the government's record in that period of time? We have had a 15 per cent increase from that period when the employment rate was stable. We now come to the month of April and note a tremendous upsurge in the unemployment rate. When we realize the tremendous increase in cost when the employment rate was nearly stable, we can see that this obviously means we are going to experience something astronomical in terms of increased cost. Let us look at the figures in actual terms of cost. Total pay-outs under unemployment insurance a year ago amounted to $3,175 million. What this really boils down to is an admission to Canadians that not only do we have to suffer the pangs of not being able to find adequate jobs in this country, but very often of not being able to find jobs of any kind. In addition, the people who are working are having to carry a tremendous burden, mainly because this government has not developed any kind of industrial strategy that allows a full degree of employment. As the amount of unemployment increases throughout the country, one thing becomes obvious, and that is that the individual who is working must carry a greater burden and pay for this additional cost. It is out of his pay cheque that these increased payments are made. As a result, these increases in unemployment and the resulting increases in unemployment insurance benefits are devastating.
What is more important than the statistical increase in the number of unemployed is the fact that for the first time in recent years we find that the people who are unemployed are those in the 25-year age group and older. Historically, the increase in unemployment has occurred when students graduating from high schools and universities have come into the labour force. That is not now the case. We are finding that those who have had jobs over the years are now becoming unemployed because of the decreasing number of jobs. People in this bracket normally were not vulnerable to unemployment. These were the people who were starting their families and for whom there was never a scarcity of employment. Traditionally, unemployment has increased when these young people have not been able to find their first job. But that is no longer the case. It is those people who have had jobs who are now becoming unemployed as a result of this general unemployment situation.
However black the picture might be painted, the fact is that we have just started to see the tip of the iceberg in the horrible situation of unemployment in this country. The fact is that we have coming into the labour market, in a month and a half, a tremendous influx of students who will not be able to find jobs. If we take the historical record of the last couple of years, we find there will be about one million students entering the labour force this year, most of whom will not find suitable employment. If we put that into percentage figures, it would give us this year between a 13 per cent and 15 per cent unemployment rate by the end of May or the start of June. That puts Canada into one of the most embarrassing and inexcusable
May 17, 1976

situations for a country with our kind of resources both natural and human. It means that an additional 130,000 people will be unemployed. If we look at a fact pointed out by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), namely, that this year, when one million students will be coming on to the labour market, only 12,000 are likely to find jobs, we find that we have underestimated the seriousness of the situation and how much it means to Canadians. This government must begin a program of incentives to encourage the private sector in our society to regain its faith and trust in the traditional enterprise systems and to get the economic show on the road again. We find that the cost of unemployment insurance is skyrocketing.
I would like to diverge for a moment because I think that as this debate carries on today we will hear many statistics relating to the number of unemployed people in percentages and on the basis of historical records. I want to place on the record an argument that is not often put forward regarding how devasting unemployment can be in the social sense. I want to point out how disheartening it can be to people with families, and how we all as Canadians end up one way or another paying for these costs associated with unemployment in additional social costs incurred by people who experience stress as a result of unemployment. A person's job is the person. We are the image of what we do. If we do nothing, our identity is shaken. Because of that we must recognize how serious it is for a person to lose his job. The ramifications of high unemployment are vastly underestimated. I should like to quote from a study which was carried out regarding the effects of unemployment and its effect on human mentality. I refer to a study carried out by Braginsky and Braginsky, who state:
Jobless men feel small, and talk the language of insignificance. Even if a new job patches up self-esteem, they still hurt from a gut-level cynicism about society.
This points out the fact that when people are unemployed in a society such as ours, they lose their self-esteem and self-respect and they also tend to blame society. We are in the midst of a debate on capital punishment, and recently we have debated law and order and violence. One thing we ought to recognize is the close correlation between the increase in violence in our society and the high unemployment rate. The study to which I referred also states the following:
Regardless of how a person becomes surplus, he or she is socially transformed. Lifestyle, expectations, goals, roles and appearance all change, and the higher one's status to begin with, the greater the impact of the social transformation. The trauma leaves a permanent scar, our research shows, long after the victim moves out of surplus status and back into the social mainstream.
This simply states that the higher one's status, the more the scar is felt at being unemployed. What is the situation in Canada today? The majority of unemployed people at present come from among those who have had jobs, not those entering the labour market for the first time. Let us look at an important factor in terms of real social harm as related to what is happening due to lack of jobs. Researcher Berkeley Rice has noted that there is a direct relationship between unemployment and suicide rates. Further,
Industrial Strategy
the number of calls received at suicide prevention centres greatly increases during periods of high unemployment. Let us look at what I think is a fairly important statement to which we should address ourselves more directly. It reads:
Not surprisingly, economic fear builds a boom in mental illness, alcoholism and suicide. The news is that government planners don't worry enough about the psychic and medical costs of recession ...
In the economic crunch, millions of American citizens worry about jobs, bills, taxes and the cost of meat. Congressmen, columnists and economists worry publicly about economic trend indicators on unemployment and inflation. But no one seems to worry much about the effect of all the worrying ...
Among the early findings of psychiatric epidemiologists was a definite inverse relationship between socio-economic status and mental illness: the lower the economic level in a given population, the greater the incidence of mental illness.
Later on, Berkeley Rice continues:
To test the relationship between economic conditions and mental illness, Brenner compared employment figures in the U.S. from 1922 to 1968 with first admissions in state mental hospitals during the same period. The results show a clear inverse relationship that holds up even for minor declines in all regions of the country: as employment drops mental hospital admissions rise. The relationships holds true whether we use employment or per capita income as the economic indicator.
This points out very clearly that it is not just a case of analysing whether we have a 6.8 or 7.4 unemployment rate, but that we should think of it in terms of the percentage of people in Canadian society who have lost jobs. We have to recognize there is a spillover. While I try to document one or two areas of the spillover, I think the cost to society is far greater than just high unemployment insurance figures, far greater even in terms of those who are under stress because they feel insignificant and have lost selfesteem because of the fact that the job is the person. When you lose your job, you lose much of your personal identity. The government, not just for economic reasons but because of its social conscience, has the obligation to society to work continually to retain a system which permits the highest rate of employment possible.
I look at Canada and ask myself what is so different between Canada and West Germany. Why is it that with our resources and human ingenuity, the kind of energy resources we have, we cannot attain full employment as do some European countries which have a much denser population than we do and whose resources are certainly no greater than ours? We have a real obligation, not just in terms of taking a look at these figures and noting that the rate of unemployment is rising or falling, but in terms of recognizing that the government has a moral obligation to society because of the stress that is placed on people when they are without jobs.
I should like to state, in conclusion, that we should address ourselves to trying to change the situation. First, we should stabilize some of the fluctuations that have occurred recently in the taxation of small business and industries. One of the feelings which I sense amongst my constituents is continual frustration-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will conclude my remarks. It is too bad that so many problems will be left to be dealt with at the end of my remarks. I believe this country should address itself to establishing a taxation system which would not entail a whole succession of rapid changes. Business people find it most frustrating because each year there are a tremendous number of changes in the taxation system. I also think that small businesses which are subject to the anti-inflation program are frustrated because of the amount of paperwork they have to do, which is reflected in their hesitation to hire people.
Another thing we must do is reassess our Unemployment Insurance Commission and its approach to paying out unemployment insurance. Surely there should be some kind of incentives program so that people are at least encouraged to work and so that welfare and unemployment insurance do not become a way of life. As long as we have a system where there is an option to work, surely we are doing nothing except being as naive as people in government who allow a system to go bn in which people can remain unemployed simply by adapting to a new lifestyle.
Not wanting to extend my time beyond the normal privilege, I will close simply by saying that the question of unemployment and lack of an industrial strategy is not just a question of charts and graphs but a question of social conscience. What is happening in Canada is that there are many people who are suffering stress, anxiety and all the ramifications which come about because jobs are so closely associated with a person's self-esteem. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on the motion brought forward by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cam-bridge (Mr. Saltsman). At the conclusion of his remarks I addressed a question to him seeking to find out whether he realized that the cabinet in fact had made a decision with respect to the White-Westinghouse application before FIRA. In his remarks, as I understood them, he indicated that he was not aware of that and was criticizing the government for not having taken a stand, but in response to the question I raised I thought he dodged it a little by agreeing that, yes indeed, they did make a decision-which was made public on March 25, 1976-but that in fact that decision did not really transfer the ownership over to General Steel Wares.
That is quite right, but the government was not considering whether GSW should or should not buy the Westing-house firm. The application really dealt with whether in fact White Consolidated should have been allowed to take over Westinghouse, and in fact that was the second time an application had been made for that purpose. The first application before FIRA was rejected on August 6, 1975, and the second rejection was on March 25, 1976.
Subsequent to that decision by the cabinet to refuse the White take-over of Westinghouse, it had been expected by many people, including myself, that this would have resulted in a rather precipitous take-over by General Steel Wares of Westinghouse. To date, that has not taken place, and as a matter of fact I have been in almost constant daily
[The Acting Speaker.]
communication with the officials of General Steel Wares to find out what the problems are in this regard. I should like to speak about that for just a moment.
It seems that the basic problem which existed at the beginning, and which prevails even to this time, is the problem about the trademark. A trademark is a register-able item under the registrar of trademarks in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. There is also another aspect; it could be viewed as a trade name as distinct from a trademark. As I understand it, a trade name is a common law right of Westinghouse Canada flowing from its use of the name "Westinghouse" in Canada and not relating to the trademark per se, which is a registerable item. It so happens that in the sale of the appliance division of Westinghouse in the United States to White, the trademark was sold. That trademark was sold in the United States on a worldwide basis. In Canada, when the application to take over was made before FIRA, it was felt that that application dealt with bricks, mortar and goodwill as spelled out in the act, and not specifically with the trademark.
I have contended all the way through in this argument that that really is not true and that the law does not really read that way, and I should like to explore this for a moment to find out whether an application before FIRA covers the whole operation which is being considered for a take-over or only part of that operation. Section 3(3) (a) of the Foreign Investment Review Act deals with all, or substantially all, of the property used in carrying on business in Canada, etc. The term "property" is dealt with in the definition section of the act, and under that definition "property" used in carrying on a business includes goodwill in connection therewith. It seems self-evident to me that the goodwill of a corporation is intrinsically tied up with the use of the name of that corporation. It seems to me that to deny that is to deny any goodwill at all to a major corporation, because the goodwill flows from the relationship which it has established over many years in dealing with consumers and the goodwill which is associated with the name draws people to buy that particular kind of product.
I think I would be right in a court of law in maintaining that goodwill in this particular case means the trade name. If there is a distinction-and I contend that there is- between the trade name and the trademark, then Westinghouse has the right to sell that trade name because the trade name has been rejected by FIRA along with all the other assets Westinghouse has in Canada. I think that is abundantly clear. The confusion in this case is that White Consolidated and Westinghouse-originally Westinghouse, U.S.A.-made a joint application before the registrar of trademarks for the registration of the name White-West-inghouse. That had not been dealt with at the time of the FIRA rejection and now a new application has gone forward on behalf of White-Westinghouse, but in this case the Westinghouse is Westinghouse Canada as distinct and different from the Westinghouse which co-operated in that earlier application.
It is alleged by some that the fact that Westinghouse Canada participated in the application before the registrar of trademarks might in some way erode the legal value which is attached or was attached to the use of the trade
May 17, 1976

name itself. This particular problem has given rise to the delay in any take-over by GSW of Westinghouse in Canada.
GSW, when making its representations to myself-and I have dealt with this question rather extensively in the past number of months-maintained that it did not want the government of Canada to indulge in any legal shenanigans or adjustments in the law which would transfer the rights to the name or the trademark to GSW. GSW simply wanted the government to do two things: first, to reject the FIRA application-and that has been done-and, second, it expressed the desire to have the government make a public statement that the government did not believe the acceptance of the application before the registrar of the trademark "Westinghouse" in the name of White was in the broad public interest and that in fact that would lead to confusion in the marketplace, which is one of the normal criteria used by the registrar in arriving at such a decision. Up to this date the government has chosen not to make that statement. I am inclined to believe that the registrar, in light of all the facts and representations which are proposed to be made to him by the employees of Westinghouse, GSW and others, will reject that application anyway.
The government is in a very difficult position, however, particularly in light of the discussion that took place over the so-called judges' affair. I gather it is really the will of parliament that the government does not express its views respecting a judicial body lest it seem to try to influence what it might or might not do. The registrar of trademarks finds himself in at least a quasi-judicial role, so I would conclude that some, if not all, members of the opposition would object if the government were to pursue the objective proposed in a convoluted way by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge.
I have no such concerns, Mr. Speaker. I think that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Mack-asey) or the Attorney General (Mr. Basford) should indicate that if the white application is rejected through FIRA, then it is inappropriate to have two users, one with the trade name Westinghouse Canada and the other, a foreign company in the United States, with the trademark Westinghouse. I would not hesitate to recommend that we make representations to the registrar of trademarks that he reject that application. In that way the whole problem of the Westinghouse deal would be solved.
I had not intended to spend too much time on this matter, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is important. The position taken by the government illustrates that the sector approach for our economic strategy to try and achieve greater Canadian ownership of our own industries is consistent, otherwise the rejection of FIRA would not have taken place because we felt it was not of significant benefit to Canada.
I should now like to deal with some other aspects of this problem. Part of our industrial strategy is our anti-inflation program. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) dealt with this at some length. There is no question that our anti-inflation program is designed to make our industries very competitive in order to save jobs
Industrial Strategy
in Canada. Although some people may argue the program is not effective, I believe we are now beginning to see results. But I think we have to reduce our own expectations and demands on the economy as well, and there is some evidence of success in this respect.
Although there seems to be a feeling that labour is being treated badly by the program, I would point out that they fare not too badly when compared with the business community. Increases in wages of from 8 per cent to 12 per cent are allowed, and historical relationships or special considerations are taken into account. In the business community there is no such generous guideline. Only increases in cost that can be justified can be passed on to the customer, and only 95 per cent of the previous five-year pretax profits are allowed. The program is a lot tougher on business than it is on labour. That effect is not well known, however, because it takes longer to become visible. We are just now beginning to see its effects.
I have been a member of a trade union for many years, Mr. Speaker, and I have a great deal of respect for unions; but I hope they begin to appreciate that we need the kind of restraint and responsibility that has been shown in England. Labour unions there got together and reduced their demands to 6 per cent, which is below the rate of inflation. This means that very realistically they are prepared to settle for less. In Canada we are not being asked to tighten our belts in that way; we are simply being asked for a reasonable, responsible approach. The most significant thing that could happen to assist our industry and to create jobs would be for labour, management and government to co-operate.
Our economic strategy has placed increased emphasis on exports and trade links. The government has taken initiatives in connection with the Pacific rim countries, Russia, China, the Common Market and Latin America, in an effort to establish appropriate trade links. Considerable progress has been made toward increasing our exports of fully and semi-manufactured goods. In 1970 we exported $11'/i billion of semi and fully manufactured goods; in 1975, we exported close to $20 billion-so the trend is in the right direction. These figures would be more impressive if we went back prior to 1970 and the institution of the auto pact, because it shifted considerable emphasis toward finished goods. If we went back even further, the increase would be much greater than the figures I have just given. I think it is important to realize we are moving in the right direction in this area of activity.
In the area of non-renewable resources, it was announced recently that more emphasis would be placed in this area of activity to promote exports of processed extracted materials as opposed to raw materials. This will take time to show benefit, but it is indication that we are following the correct policy.
The government's determination to become self-supporting through oil production is an important part of an industrial strategy. Unless we do this, in time we will become the victim of the high prices set by the countries from whom we have to buy. This, of course, places our industries and our workers in a poor position. We need to take out some insurance to guarantee the future development of oil, the new pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal, a delivery system and a capacity to produce our own fuel,
9S568-26

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
which is a key element in any reasonable industrial strategy.
We should also consider the question of Canadian ownership of our resources and industries. In this connection may I allude to the activities of the Foreign Investment Review Agency which has been of some help. When one considers the establishment of Petro-Canada, Canada Development Corporation and similar corporations, one will see that the government is acting on all fronts to making certain we become more self-reliant and exercise ever more control over our own economic destiny. It is important to note this.
May I say a word about the Canada Development Corporation, which is a public corporation in which Canadians will be allowed to purchase shares and so participate in the development of the nation. At this point the company's capital stock is $565 million. There are 100 million class A shares, 322 million common shares, 142 million class B voting shares; retained earnings at this moment total $42 million, and the surplus of the Canada Development Corporation stands at $51 million. It is a healthy corporation which has invested in Polysar and Connaught Laboratory holdings, both of which it owns to the extent of 100 per cent. It has bought into Petrosar to the tune of 20 per cent, and Texas Gulf to the tune of 30 per cent, and owns 100 per cent of CDC oil and gas.
