speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members. I will not be long and will deal with but two or three other highlights. As we are talking of industrial strategy, it would be inappropriate not to draw to the attention of Parliament our new competition policy, phase one of which is already being implemented. It goes a long way to ensuring genuine competition in society. Further steps must be taken, but what has been done is particularly important to businessmen. Many people look on competition policy as important to the consumer, which it is; but it is also important to small and medium-sized businessmen: it will make sure they are not put out of business by the large, multinational corporations. The government's policy in this regard is a giant step forward in the right direction in terms of economic strategy. Other steps will be taken when phase two of the competition policy is introduced. These, too, will be found helpful in the area of activity with which we are concerned.
May I mention briefly the new Canadian corporations' legislation which has done much to protect the investors of this country and will encourage our investors to invest in Canadian corporations. The legislation provides the minimum protection needed and will ensure that Canadians may invest with confidence in Canadian enterprises. The legislation has cut out much red tape in the incorporating of federally-incorporated businesses. That will help the businessmen of this country. Perhaps we should go fur-

ther, to remove some of the impediments or some of the negative aspects, let us say, concerning Canadian businessmen. I refer, for example, to the multiplicity of forms to do with UIC, social insurance, and so on, which take up the time of businessmen. I feel that the departments of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Industry, Trade and Commerce and others should get together and see what can be done to minimize the numbers of forms, etc., which businessmen are required to complete, so that instead of providing this free service to the government our businessmen can spend more time increasing productivity.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is involved with many programs of research and development which will enhance productivity. I spoke about these at some length a couple of days ago in the House of Commons. Also, we must do what we can to help the businesses of this country compete with international businesses or corporations based in other countries.
Lastly, may I draw the attention of the House to programs of manpower retraining, on-the-job training, and so on, which the federal government instituted in an attempt to match the capabilities of our work force with the requirements of the business community. Such programs are most important. One cannot consider unemployment and industrial strategy without taking into account the necessity of upgrading the skills of our work force and matching those skills with the needs of society.
I thank the House for its indulgence, Mr. Speaker. I wished to say more but will not as I do not wish to abuse the privilege granted to me. I conclude by saying that an industrial strategy we need, and an industrial strategy we have. If we implement that strategy broadly-and I have dealt with some of the possibilities-we shall do something worth while for industry and the workers of this country and solve some of our immediate difficulties.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), a member of the NDP, for bringing forward the motion we are considering on this allotted day. The subject is timely and appropriate. It is timely to talk about Canada's industrial strategy. Certainly, the subject is not new, but old. If my recollection is correct, the issue of industrial strategy arose late in the 1960s. We heard about industrial strategy from a previous Liberal government. Responding to criticisms being levelled at it in connection with tight money and the difficulties besetting certain sectors of the economy, the government of that day said conditions would improve because it was working on an industrial strategy. It was to bring forward an industrial strategy which would solve this nation's problems. After the phrase caught the ears of the media and the people of the country, the government became squeamish. In the throne speech debate of January, 1973, the then minister of industry, trade and commerce, now the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), did his best to dissociate himself from that phrase. As reported on page 151 of Hansard for May 10, 1973, he said in part:
I am simply being a little more realistic when I talk about the government's so-called industrial strategy as being directed more toward the development and elaboration of a coherent set of industrial policies for Canada rather than the almost impossible task of producing a master plan.
May 17, 1976

Evidently the government of that day had abandoned the goal of drafting a master plan for Canadian industrial strategy. Instead, it wanted to develop what the minister called a coherent set of industrial policies. He outlined the government's program during that debate and later elaborated on the development of this so-called coherent set of industrial policies. The minister emphasized three areas which he, then as minister of industry, trade and commerce, would treat as being of top priority. They were trade, aid to small business, and foreign investment.
Let us consider what has happened. What progress did the minister make in pursuing his three priority goals? Consider the question of foreign investment. As the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge said earlier, and other speakers agreed with him, Canada is in the unenviable position of being the nation in the world with the largest proportion of its industries foreign-owned. That is a sad situation which concerns the majority of Canadians. But it need never have come about. The government said it would take firm action in this area. What did it do? It created the Foreign Investment Review Agency, that is all. Thus far, as I see it, the main accomplishment of this agency has been the creation of a new industry. It has created work for lawyers, a new specialty in law. For a law firm to call itself established or competent it must have within its ranks an expert on the Foreign Investment Review Agency, in the same way that it must have experts on tax, estates, and so on. A whole new area of work has been created for lawyers and accounts, but little else.
Any dispassionate examination of the percentage of Canadian industry which is foreign-owned shows nothing has changed. If anything, it has become worse. It is not surprising that anything should happen. Our high degree of foreign ownership is a direct consequence of previous Liberal administration industrial strategies. There was the strategy of C. D. Howe when he was minister of trade and commerce-and I guess minister of everything which was to encourage foreign investment. The policy of the government was to encourage foreign investment. That was the way to create jobs in this country. That was the way the government foresaw that we could import the foreign technology which we needed. It must be obvious to even the most simple mind that if you are going to alter the consequence of this policy which has been in effect for many years, you must do more than just put up obstacles to increased foreign investment; you must take positive steps to encourage replacement with Canadian investment.
C. D. Howe's policy was designed to create jobs. That job creation is even more necessary today when we have record levels of unemployment. The Canadian people have stated emphatically that they do not want to gain this increased employment solely through the importation of foreign branch plants because in the long run the costs are too large. Has this government done anything in a positive way to bring about the Canadian investment necessary to create these jobs? If so, they have disguised it very well because it is certainly not evident.
This government has brought in things which have had the opposite effect. One example is the capital gains tax. What incentive is there to invest in Canada? There is another side of the argument to capital gains tax. That is equity of taxation. There is no question about it. I hope
Industrial Strategy
that someone on the opposite side is at least looking at the possibility of indexing that taxation for inflation. The combination of inflation and capital gains means that investment in the stocks of Canadian companies is simply not worth while. It is the foolish investor indeed who puts his money in that investment vehicle.
The second big item of priority that the minister talked about is aid to small businesses. He said this was going to be given priority consideration by his ministry which spends some $240 million a year. He talked about six new initiatives: increased financial help to small businesses through the Industrial Development Bank, other granting programs, counselling for small businesses, stronger regional offices in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, aids to facilitate technology transferred to small business, and special emphasis on tourism.
One could go into a great deal of discussion about each of those six initiatives. However, I would be willing to bet any amount that for every small businessman in Canada who has been helped by these government programs, it is possible to find ten small businesses that have been hurt, and hurt badly, by this government through its programs. Every member of parliament has a file full of letters from small businessmen in their constituencies complaining about the detrimental effects upon them as a result of one or another of the government's programs.
The third area, and this was given first priority by the minister in terms of the initiatives this government would take in the years following the 1973 throne speech, related to trade. This area was going to be given top consideration. The government was really going to get after the question of trade. In 1973 they had a surplus, or favourable trade balance of $1,327 million. After the enhancing activity by this ministry and government, and after priority consideration being given to it, our trade balance went from plus to minus-$2,440 million overall.
If you look at the high technology, manufactured goods which fall within the purview of this minister, in other words eliminating agriculture and raw materials which are Energy, Mines and Resources, the performance is far worse. In 1973, for example, we had a high technology trade deficit of over $5 billion. In 1975 this had gone to over $8 billion. That was the disastrous performance after three years of this government saying they were going to give it very high priority.
Those sectors of the economy that have not been given high priority should be thankful. They should be grateful that this government has not given them high priority as they, too, may have suffered as badly as our high technology industries. Performance has deteriorated tremendously since the minister announced this coherent set of industrial policies. Our unemployment rates are at a record high, trade represents a record deficit, foreign ownership has become worse, regional disparities are worse, and there are record losses due to strikes. No industrialized country has lost more time due to strikes than Canada. The gross national product is up. However, Canada used to have the highest GNP per population, the so called standard of living. We are now sixth in the world. Under this government we moved from first to sixth. That is performance!
It is comparatively easy to articulate all the problems and mistakes of this government. They are obvious and many. Canada is well blessed with several independent
95 5 68-2614

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
bodies outside of government which examine Canada's economy. There are groups such as the Economic Council, the Conference Board, the C. D. Howe Research Institute, the Chambers of Commerce, the Canadian Association of Independent Banks, and so on. Virtually every one of these bodies, looking at Canadian industry, has reached the conclusion, in contrast to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who is standing in this afternoon for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), that all is not well. Things are not as rosy within Canadian industry as that minister has described them. Government policies are not exclusively at fault in this regard, but they certainly are not helping to cure the problems. In many instances they are directly causing them.
For example, one of the common themes in analyses of Canada's economy by groups outside government is a call for more innovation, more productivity from Canadian industry. Increasing productivity, as the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge has pointed out, is not a question of getting labour to work harder; it comes from better ways of doing things, better organization, improved technique, better technology. What has the government done in terms of increasing productivity? Well, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has indicated several times during the question period that he has some kind of brains trust locked away in this office looking into the question. Apart from that, I know of nothing else which has been done to improve Canada's record in this field.
Increased productivity, as we all know, results from better management and improved technology. As the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) has pointed out, management in Canadian business is beset with government bureaucracy, with forms and with demands upon its time. Five or six years back, one of the leading Canadian business magazines carried out a survey and reached the conclusion that 35 per cent of executive time is spent dealing with government, filling out forms, answering questionnaires, accommodating demands made upon them by the civil service. Since then the situation has undoubtedly become worse. I need only call attention to the demands of the Anti-Inflation Board, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and Statistics Canada, which is day by day requiring more and more information so as to employ the
4,000	or 5,000 people who are to occupy that building across the river.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Let us do away with it, then, as we did with Information Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
There are some positive notes to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais). In general, far from being aided by government programs, Canadian business management is being severely hampered. As for improved technology, only last Thursday there was a full-scale debate in this House during which speakers from all opposition parties were in agreement that the government had done nothing worth while to improve the productivity of Canadian industry in the field of technology. Yet in the long run that is the only answer.

Let us see how other government policies have worked out. Supposedly, as part of a coherent industrial strategy, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was set up to broaden the base of industrial development across the country. Compare the policies of this department, in the course of whose development vast sums of money were spent, with the policy followed by the Department of Transport and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to say nothing of the Department of Supply and Services. One gets the impression, Mr. Speaker, that they are adversaries working in completely opposite directions.
In conclusion, may I say that no country in the world has the combination of resources which we in Canada enjoy. We have the natural resources, we have a well-educated people, we have a truly democratic system of government, and we have a free enterprise system. It would be a tragedy for Canada and for the world if we failed to meet our potential. There is no need to fail. A coherent set of industrial policies, an industrial strategy which while interfering less would provide incentives for Canadians, permitting them to pursue the goals they chose, would in itself be almost sufficient to ensure success. It is tragic to see a government, apparently with good motives, being so wrong-headed, so persistent in pursuing, on an ad hoc basis, the measures it has adopted, thereby denying Canadians the type of country they all desire and which they are capable of achieving.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to take part in the debate today. In the past few weeks we have been discussing issues of conscience, such as capital punishment, which in the long run really involve some six or seven persons a year under the definition of first degree murder. Today I am indebted to the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) for introducing what I consider to be a motion reflecting one of the most important issues confronting our society, one which affects not just a few people but many millions. I refer to lack of a national industrial and employment program.
Since this country was founded, and even before it officially became a nation, the predominant economic theory, indeed, the predominant practice, was that of laissez-faire. Perhaps in those far off days it worked, though I am still not sure that it did. But I believe we must put the motion before us into some sort of historical perspective. I should like to go back to the post-civil war era in the United States, the era of reconstruction in which the Americans sought to rebuild their country and indeed did so most successfully, but based upon a different kind of economic system. It was capitalist, no doubt about that, but when they went to the money markets in Europe and Great Britain and asked for capital for their canals, their railroads, their telegraph lines, their manufacturing industries, they included a proviso: it had to be bond capital-in other words, non-voting capital. They succeeded. They got the money from Europe, but since it was in the form of bond capital they were able to control the way in which the money was used.
What happened in Canada from the time of John A. Macdonald, with his tariff policies and transportation policies, with the development of manufacturing in the east and primarily farm production in the west, was that we did
May 17, 1976

not get bond capital so as to maintain control over our future development in economic terms. They were willing to take anything, and successive governments accepted equity capital, which meant control over our economy passing to outside interests. So at the outset of these remarks I should like to put the historical situation into perspective. I wish to state at the outset, also, that the economy here developed differently from that of the United States in another sense. It developed as a combination of public and private enterprise. I suppose we really have not had a national policy on industrial growth and development since John A. Macdonald in the late 1800s. Unwittingly-and I am not blaming our first rate prime ministers-this tariff wall created a branch plant economy in this country. Instead of trying to knock down this wall, they jumped over it and built industries in this country that served the people and investors of the United States to a far greater degree than the people of this country. All during the 1880s, 1890s and up to the First World War, and indeed after the First World War when we finally became a country in substance as well as in name, this kind of equity capital domination continued through successive Conservative and Liberal governments, and I think it is a problem from which we are still suffering today.
[DOT] <1710)
The second thing I should like to put into perspective is the hue and cry that has gone out across the country about the negative effects of unemployment insurance. I have very mixed feelings about the UIC. In fact, I would not mind a bit if private insurance companies got together and ran the whole thing themselves. Of course, hon. members know what would happen then; premiums would triple or quadruple and benefits would be halved, because they would have to make a profit. Are the unemployed, especially the 80 per cent of our unemployment who have no job through no fault of their own but, rather, because the government over there does not have a full employment policy, to be blamed for unemployment? That is the first question.
The other matter that bothers me about unemployment resulting from not having an employment and industrial development policy is that the stop-gap social assistance programs are, in effect, institutionalizing poverty. This institutionalization of poverty, with all its handouts, is making capitalism respectable and acceptable. On the one hand, corporations grab every cent they can from the government. But who is to be blamed for the failure of our social assistance programs? It is not the con artists in the boardrooms of this country, but the little con artists who are trying to rip off our social assistance programs. To me this is reprehensible and unacceptable.
We must take a more appropriate approach to those who work in our industrial complex in this country. Who really makes the major decisions affecting our economy and industries? Is it those who have been laid off temporarily, or is it those who work for eight weeks and then try to rip off the Unemployment Insurance Commission? How many of the 761,000 people who are unemployed today in this country are unemployed because they want to be unemployed? People come to my constituency office Saturday after Saturday and ask me to find them a job, Mr. Speaker. They have gone to Manpower but have been unsuccessful.
Industrial Strategy
Employers go to Manpower and are also unsuccessful. I suggest to the members of this House that those responsible for unemployment in this country include, to begin with, the Department of Finance, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks and corporate boardrooms of this nation. These are the people with the economic and political power to act.
What has been the record of this government over the past several years? It has been pretty dismal. It is true we are producing jobs, but as we produce them more and more fall outside the labour market. Probably half of the 761,000 people out of work now will never find gainful employment again. I heard a member a moment ago say that the answer to this problem is the rationalization of industry and employment, that with increasing technological change we should modernize equipment. That may be true, but in the long run, what does it do? It puts more people out of work. Let me give the House an example that occurred a few weeks ago in southwestern Ontario. The CNR ran its turbotrain at a speed somewhere in the neighbourhood of 140 miles an hour.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: That was in eastern Ontario.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Yes, I believe between Toronto and Montreal. I realize energy is not touched on in the motion, but when they ran this train at 140 miles an hour, the CNR employed their own workers to stand at underpasses or overpasses along the route to warn cars as the train went whistling through. Yet at the same time the government claims we cannot afford to build overpasses, underpasses, subways or whatever you want to call them. This was a perfect example of how we could put unskilled people to work and pay them a decent wage rather than putting them on unemployment insurance. These people are waiting for a job that is probably not there for them.
This motion relates, at the moment indirectly, but I feel within the next few weeks or months will relate most directly, to a major industry in the city of Brantford which I have the honour to represent. The situation I am about to relate is not an isolated one but is similar to other cases which my hon. friend and colleague from Waterloo-Cam-bridge mentioned in his speech earlier this afternoon. In the city of Brantford there is a farm implements manufacturing company known as White's Farm Equipment. It is a subsidiary of the White Motor Corporation of the United States. For the last couple of years it has been further and further under. Indeed, in its last quarterly report for 1975 it was $60 million belly up. A man named Ed Reddick is chairman of the board of White Consolidated Industries, which has nothing to do with White Motors; it just happens to have the same name. Reddick has a history of buying out corporations that are about to go broke or which at least are in very serious financial straits. As reported in the American Press, his reputation includes that of stripping subsidiaries, closing down sales offices, firing sales personnel and at least minimizing, if not totally eliminating, scientific research. He boasts about this.

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
On May 3, White Consolidated Industries was to have a directors' meeting. Everything was laid out in the press that he was about to buy out White Motors, of which the White Farm Equipment Company of Brantford, the Euclid Earth Moving Equipment Company, and I do not know the exact name of it, of St. Catharines, and White Trucks, I believe of British Columbia, are subsidiaries. He boasts about the fact that he can, in his terms, rationalize industries. As far as I am concerned, this means buying them out, dismantling them for what he can get out of it and then moving on to some other corporation nearly bankrupt.
Fortunately for the White Farm Equipment Company of Brantford, Mr. Reddick took ill the night before, on May 2, and as far as I know he is still in the hospital. At the shareholders' meeting of WCI his argument to buy out White Motors, so I am told, lost by a bare two votes. Somebody might say in opposition that this is hypothetical because it has not happened. The point is that it is all there in black and white. This was his intention. White Farm Equipment in Brantford employs 600 to 700 employees. In 1969 or 1970 Reddick pulled the same trick. It was not the Canadian government that made him renege and go back and not buy out White Motors Industries in the United States. It was the United States government that said he could not do it even after the deal had gone through. It was not our tough guys over there-no way. It was the United States government that said he could not go ahead with it.
Unfortunately, while he had control of the White Motor Company and its subsidiaries in Canada, people were laid off. Workers at what was then called White Cockshutt in Brantford were laid off, and some of them had seniority back to 1947. I might add that Cockshutt, White-Cockshutt and now White Farm Equipment in Brantford, has had excellent relations with their employees. They have not had a strike, to my knowledge, since just after the Second World War.
At the time Mr. Reddick was trying to implement the buying out of this corporation, the buying out of the subsidiaries and stripping them for what he could get out of them. He would cut out the science and technology end, or the creative and technological end, and to hell with the Canadian workers. The fact that a small town in southwestern Ontario with a population of 65,000 was losing 700 jobs did not make any difference to a man like Reddick. He runs his empire from the United States, or it could be from Japan, Great Britain, France or West Germany. What I am really saying, and I hope I am distilling it to the one incident, because I think this one incident encompasses what the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge said in his opening remarks today, is that without a national industrial strategy over which Canadians have control, this is the kind of thing that can happen.
Without this kind of industrial strategy for government, private enterprise and public enterprise, this kind of White Consolidated Industries attempted take-over will continue-and we cannot afford that in this country. We do not have to be rabid nationalists, saying we do not like Americans and we do not like American capital or capital from any other part of the world. What we need is some control over the destiny of our future economy. If we do not have this-and we do not at the present time-there is some-

thing wrong not only with the government but with every member of this House.
I do not think you have to be a Liberal, a Conservative, a New Democrat or a Creditiste to stand on your feet and say that the global village is getting smaller and we have to co-operate. Interdependence among nations is becoming a most important aspect of life itself. But at the same time we have the right to speak for ourselves in economic and industrial matters. This is the important thing. Otherwise we will be looked upon and laughed at as the second or third cousins of the most powerful nation in the world. That is not an anti-American statement. It is our own governments over the years which have allowed this to happen.
I only heard part of the speech of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and I am subject to correction in respect of what he said. He mentioned that one of our problems in respect of unemployment today resulted from the number of women in the employment market. If we had a economy in this country and a national industrial strategy that provided enough jobs so we had full employment, and so those who work, whether in factories or offices, received a decent income on which they could live comfortably, not luxuriously, I daresay half those women would not have to be part of the unemployed work force today or, indeed, the 2 per cent I believe the minister said who are working. We would not need that, and we would probably have a better social climate in this country in which mothers would stay home and raise their families. It is precisely because of our lack of a national industrial policy that these women and mothers have to go out to work. I do not see how the minister's argument is valid.
I see that my time has pretty well run out. I would simply like to reiterate what I said a few minutes ago. Unless FIR A begins to act, and unless part II of the bill becomes operative in an effective way, particularly in the energy field, we are not going to have a kind of economy in this country in which we can exercise an independent posture and an enlightened posture in the world force.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it somewhat ironic and amusing that the last speaker, a member of the NDP, in his closing remarks should have used the expression "what we need are controls." The opposition argument on the motion which we are debating today, dealing with industrial strategy, has dealt extensively with recession statistics and trends in an attempt to paint a gloomy picture. Inflation and unemployment at current levels are cause for concern. Nevertheless, arguments should be kept in perspective.
Is it imagined that Canada, one-tenth the size or the power of the United States, could have come through unscathed when the world economy is going through its worst upheaval since the Second World War? The year 1975 was, without doubt, the most difficult year for the government and the country since the end of the war. In a country dependent on imports for one third of its needs, and needing to export a similar proportion of its goods and services to maintain its standard of living, it is surely remarkable that we in Canada have been able to avoid the acute hardships that the recession has caused in other countries.
This dependency on other countries for exports and imports makes it impossible for us to immunize ourselves from world influences. Our situation has been aggravated more recently on the domestic front by the reluctance of corporations, union leadership, and various levels of government to accept the effects of recession. The demands, not just to maintain the status quo but to obtain improvements over their positions in previous years, have exerted tremendous pressures on those not able to join together to form a pressure group. Federal government action, however reluctant, to control inflation, became inevitable when a voluntary consensus was so bluntly refused. Surely 1975 was not the year to demand the highest increases in prices and salaries.
The key to beating inflation was and still is productivity. The mover of the motion complains that it is not the fault of the worker that productivity falls. Does he seriously suggest that those same companies that he accuses of profit motivation would not be happy to see increased productivity as a balancing factor to decreasing demand and falling prices?
Industrial Strategy
One of the easier ways to alleviate the effects of recession is for everyone to minimize lost time by strikes and to improve efficiency by two or three percentage points.
However, it is important to maintain a reasonable perspective. Economic conditions in Canada are certainly a cause for concern and deserve the full individual attention of the government. Nevertheless, having illustrated the world influence on the Canadian economy, it is appropriate to make comparisons with conditions elsewhere.
Unemployment rates and unused productive capacity in the major industrialized countries rose during the first half of 1975 to levels unprecedented in the post war period. For OECD countries combined real GNP declined at an annual rate of about 5 per cent during the first half of 1975, the third consecutive half year of decline, with the low point reached about mid-year.
For example, while the percentage change in real GNP for 1975 as compared with 1974 increased in Canada by 0.2 per cent, there was a decrease in France of 2 per cent, in Germany of 4 per cent, in the United Kingdom of 2 per cent, and in the United States of 3 per cent.

If we take in consideration the effects of inflation, it seems that the Canadian economy reached a peak during the first months of 1973 beginning a slight recession since 1974 up to the end of 1975. Of course, Canadian productivity has been clearly below normal between 1973-75, but we should compare our conditions with those of the United States. That country is by far our most important trading partner and the cyclical behaviour of the Canadian economy normally closely follows the American economy.
The comparisons are based on production, employment, unemployment, costs and prices, foreign sector, capital expenditures and development of the GNP per inhabitant. It follows that the United States experienced a much more serious recession than Canada between 1973-75, as shown by the comparative movements of real production, employment, unemployment and investments. At the same time, the Canadian experience was less propitious in two important sectors: first the unit costs of labour in manufacturing and, second, the foreign sector.
If the productivity of American manufacturers was still less propitious than that of their Canadian counterparts since 1973, this disadvantage has been substantially offset by smaller salary increases. There clearly results a temporary degradation at least of the competitive status of the Canadian manufacturing industry as to the unit costs of manpower compared with those in the United States. Canada has experienced since 1973 a quick degradation of its merchandizing and current accounts while the contrary was true in the United States which is mostly due to a greatly reduced demand from abroad.

The period since 1973 has seen a closer convergence in per capita GNP in Canada and the United States. Between 1973 and 1975 Canada's GNP output in current dollars climbed by about 29 per cent, or nearly twice as fast as in the United States. In 1975 per capita GNP in Canada has climbed to within about 3 percentage points of that in the United States, compared with a gap of about 11 per cent in 1973. In real terms, Canada's GNP output advanced by

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
about 3 per cent. This is well below the normal growth rate of at least 9 per cent in an average two year period. However, in the U.S. real GNP was actually 4 per cent lower in 1975 than in 1973.
The GNP price deflator, the broadest measure of over-all price change in the economy, advanced by 25 per cent over a two year period in Canada, or somewhat faster than the 19 per cent increase in the United States during the same period of time. The volume of industrial production declined by somewhat more than 2 per cent in Canada between 1973 and 1975, compared with a decline of 9.4 per cent in the U.S.
Retail sales in Canada climbed by 32 per cent in the two years ending in 1975, compared with an increase of half this rate in the United States. Housing starts declined by 14 per cent in Canada during the last two years, compared with a 43 per cent drop in the United States. The Canadian labour force climbed by about 8 per cent in the past two years, a rate nearly twice as fast as the 4.4 per cent advance in the United States. Total employment growth in Canada advanced by 6.4 per cent despite the economic slowdown in the past two years. In the U. S. it climbed by less than half of one per cent.
As far as the manufacturing sector is concerned, the decline in the volume of Canadian manufacturing of about 2.5 per cent was only one third as steep as the decline in the United States. There was also a sharper drop off in the average weekly hours in U.S. manufacturing. Output per man hour in Canadian manufacturing advanced by 3.3 per cent between 1973 and 1975, or nearly three times the rate experienced in the United States. However, average hourly earnings in Canadian manufacturing climbed by more than 31 per cent in the most recent two year period, compared with only 18 per cent in the United States. The result was that unit labour costs in Canadian manufacturing advanced by 27 per cent compared with 16.5 per cent in the United States as the comparative advantage in Canadian productivity was more than matched by a steeper climb in wages.
As I pointed out earlier in my remarks, a more responsible attitude in relating wage and salary demands to productivity rather than to anticipated increases in the inflation rate could have moderated, to a considerable extent, the high inflation which necessitated the antiinflation legislation.
I shall conclude my remarks with a reference to one of the improving sectors of our economy, the growth of Canada's consulting and technical service industries in international markets. Consulting and technical service industries contribute more than $1 billion annually to the Canadian economy; over $150 million in fees alone was earned from foreign contracts in 1974.
Capital equipment exports follow where our Canadian consultants have contracts. Canadian technology is in great demand abroad, and frequently our expertise parallels the needs of developing countries. This consulting expertise is in a multitude of fields, including communications, transportation, forestry, resource development, and power development. The industry is largely Canadian owned; it is aggressive and entrepreneurial. The Canadian

consultant is taking the lead in the pursuit of capital project business abroad.
In closing, whilst one cannot be surprised that during a slowdown period in the Canadian economy the purveyors of doom come out in force, a more balanced assessment of the true picture would indicate that we in Canada have performed relatively well in comparison with the rest of the world. Certainly we always have a need to improve, but a more positive attitude and a little more pride in our accomplishments will help us to attain our common objectives.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are grateful for the opportunity provided by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) today with respect to the subject matter of unemployment which, if anything, has been a consistent concern of hon. members of this House on all sides.
There has been a continued recurrence of high unemployment throughout the country. However, those of us who come from the Atlantic provinces, when faced with either statistical figures or with the latest reports on unemployment, realize that this is not something new but something we have long experienced in our part of the country. Indeed it has been recognized for quite a number of years, certainly since the early 1960's, that the federal government has a basic responsibility with respect to the continuing high levels of unemployment which have existed in certain areas of the country, those areas which have, to use the popular phrase, suffered from regional economic and social disparity.
While the motion before us today refers specifically to the general unemployment situation which exists, a rate of 7.4 per cent-or in terms of actual Canadians without jobs, some 761,000-I think it is incumbent upon us in this debate to realize that the problem has been particularly acute in two areas which I want to mention quite specifically. One area comprises the four Atlantic provinces which have traditionally experienced unemployment in rates at sometimes double and, in a number of instances, triple that of the national average. It is a situation which no member or minister should want to accept happily for one moment, but I think we have to be frank and recognize that the general experience to date in attempting to deal with this problem has not been overly satisfactory.
I did not hear the minister when he made his comments with respect to the problems of unemployment as he saw them from his perspective as Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), but from what I have learned about his speech it strikes me that it was a speech which generally tried to make excuses for what presently is the situation rather than to give some suggestion or indication as to what steps the government will be taking to alleviate this problem.
Surely it is not something which was sprung on the government as brand new information with the last report from Statistics Canada. It seems to me that for as long as this minister has been in office, and certainly since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been in office, it has been an almost constant complaint that the problem of
May 17, 1976

unemployment in Canada has not been dealt with satisfactorily.
However, the two specific groups which concern me today and which have suffered unduly due to the lack of an industrial strategy are undoubtedly the people who live in areas of economic and social disparity such as those in the Atlantic provinces, part of the province of Quebec, certain parts of northern Ontario, and northwestern Canada.
I also think particularly of a group which is equally important but not quite so easily identifiable, the young people in our society, in terms of the long term damage which we have done with respect to the most important resource which exists for Canada, and that is their future positive attitude and ability to participate in the ongoing life of this country.
If there is a major and compelling criticism above all else which can be made about this government in the employment field, it is, quite frankly, the betrayal of an opportunity for employment which should be, but has not been, available for many thousands-indeed, hundreds of thousands-of young people in our society. I know this only too well because during my times here as a member I have had the opportunity to consider in detail some of the specific responses the government has made with respect to youth unemployment.
Many years ago on the occasion of one particular bad set of published statistics, or a report from Statistics Canada with respect to the high percentage of unemployed young people, those under the age of 24, the Prime Minister indicated to me in an answer that he too was concerned about the problem, and for that reason the government at that time established a high powered interdepartmental committee which was to take seriously the problem of the long term high incidence of youth unemployment.
What have been the results of that self-professed interest in this serious social problem? The results have been nil. Of course there have been experiments with respect to the Opportunities for Youth program, but that program has gone the way of all flesh. The government announced it as an interim measure to deal with what it perceived to be a very serious situation. One is not sure that it was attempting to deal with the reality of that situation or merely the seeming politics of it, but Opportunities for Youth is no longer in existence.
A program which was introduced by the Prime Minister's predecessor as a Canadian response to the then popular American Peace Corps was the Company of Young Canadians. The Company of Young Canadians had its difficulties, and no one would disagree that it was instituted at a time of very serious social unrest. However, I think hon. members on either side who have looked at the work which was done, particularly in latter years, by the Company of Young Canadians, have to be impressed both by the dedication of the young people who were involved and by the extent to which they were actually able to assist in the development of self-help programs in a number of disadvantaged communities across the country, and for a very small price, I might add, because as hon. members know the budgetary item for the Company of Young Canadians was quite small in comparison with many activities funded by the government. What was the
Industrial Strategy
response to this particular innovation? It was given the axe. One opportunity for channeling some of the energy and idealism and even the anxiety of young people was destroyed. They could have been a positive force in the real social and economic development of the country.
As I said in another place on another occasion, the government is somewhat like its present energy program- it has run out of gas. I suppose the obvious thing to say is that the sooner it can be replaced, the better. An enormous number of young people have become very cynical and frustrated by what they perceive to be the government's lack of interest in their problems of employment and effective participation in our society.
I see one hon. member shake his head. I am not sure whether he is opposed to dealing with the chronic, high unemployment that faces our young people or whether he is sharing in the collective fatigue that exists in this administration. Either is an extreme condition and should not be tolerated any longer.
I am amazed at the government's lack of sensitivity, its lack of an industrial strategy or indeed any strategy to deal with the employment of such a resource as the young people of this country. This aspect of the matter deserves much more time, Mr. Speaker, but I want to deal with another aspect of unemployment which I consider equally grave, and that is the situation in the Atlantic provinces.
It is perhaps a fact of our experience as representatives that, because we have been faced with high unemployment figures so consistently in the last few years, we have ceased to be alarmed by the extent of unemployment in our own communities. Recently I saw the latest published unemployment figures for the Atlantic provinces. It was interesting to compare the reports from the Manpower offices to see how closely they checked with the figures published by Statistics Canada.
The national unemployment rate is 7.6 per cent. In Newfoundland, it is 16.3 per cent; in Prince Edward Island, 13.4 per cent; Nova Scotia, 10.3 per cent, and New Brunswick, 13.2 per cent. This means that in the Atlantic provinces unemployment is running at double the national average.
On a year to year basis a comparison of the number of people registered with the Manpower Centres in the Atlantic provinces is quite shocking. In March last year 4,196 people were registered with the Manpower Centre in Charlottetown; this year the figure jumped to 5,600. In Summer-side 4,200 people were registered in March of last year as actively looking for employment; this year the figure climbed to 6,007, a growth of 43 per cent. These are not figures that one can accept in a sanguine manner when one realizes the hardship and heartbreak experienced by heads of households who must report to their families week after week that there is still no job available. It is difficult for us to identify with a figure in the hundreds of thousands of unemployed. But when I meet people in my constituency who are denied productive employment, Mr. Speaker, then I know the tragedy of the lack of an industrial policy on the part of the government.
It is incredible that in the Atlantic provinces the government should masquerade behind a program of regional expansion. In 1969, when various programs and policies

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
were put together to create a department that was going to deal directly with the under-employed and unemployed in specific regions, we were optimistic. In 1976, however, the department only administers patchwork programs that basically do nothing about the unemployment problem in the Atlantic provinces. In Charlottetown last week the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) said-and I hope I quote him closely enough not to misrepresent him-that during a time of restraint we must not expect that anything can be done effectively to offset that with respect to regional economic programs and policies. He has said similar things in the House in reply to questions about rate increases of 100 per cent on the main ferry link to the mainland and the repeated requests from the Canadian National Railways for an increase in basic freight rates, which of course would effect the cost of moving basic goods out of our region.
It is incredible that the government would establish a department to alleviate regional disparities and then have its own energy and transportation policies, tariff policies, and restraint policies go totally against it and undermine any achievement it might have gained. What kind of credibility can this establish with respect to an industrial policy for the country or for areas where the government has an important and special responsibility?
I may need to say a few additional words at eight o'clock because I think this is a very important subject. At this time, however, I would respectfully call it six o'clock.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that before we adjourned for supper I was trying to deal with what I perceived to be two of the most consistent and offensive areas of high unemployment which have existed in this country for a number of years, almost totally during the time the present government has been in office. One has to do with the shockingly high numbers of young people unemployed, more than 14 per cent at last count; and the other has to do with consistent and chronically high unemployment in areas like the Atlantic provinces where, on a regional average, unemployment is at well over 14 per cent.
I will not repeat, for which hon. members on all sides will be grateful, what I said before supper, but I want to emphasize that, as the motion suggests, there is indeed no industrial strategy to counteract the very serious and high unemployment which exists today. In fact if there is any one criticism I have of this motion, it is that it does not go far enough.
I believe that if we are to deal with the problem of regional unemployment the time has long since passed when we should realize that it is not sufficient to have a

series of particular programs or, indeed, one department trying to carry and develop matters of responsibility in this particular area. I mentioned before the supper adjournment the failure to introduce consistent and supportive policies in areas of tremendous importance to the Atlantic regions, areas such as energy and transportation. I will not go into detail, but it seems to me that there has been a tremendous deterioration in that there has been a lack of support from the department in dealing with both energy and transportation. Indeed much if not all that is being attempted under regional disparity programs sponsored by DREE is undermined by the lack of consistent and co-ordinated programs in the totality of federal government intervention in the Atlantic provinces.
At present it seems to me that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is indeed a prisoner of the government, unable to make its weight felt fully in the activities of other departments when dealing with the problems of unemployment and under-employment in the Atlantic provinces.
On the question of young people it seems that our approach has not been comprehensive. It is a well known fact that the provinces have a vital stake in the whole question of youth opportunity, and employment, but there has been literally no effective consultation with the provinces on this question. The relationship existing between education, manpower training, and job opportunities for young people has been totally ignored by the government.
As I said, if I have any criticism of the motion presented today by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge it is that it only deals with industrial strategy affecting employment. It seems to me that we need, in real terms, a totally new economic and social policy, one whose basic commitment is to full employment. I remember a few years ago when the late president of Queen's University, a man of tremendous stature, Dr. John Deutsch, told a parliamentary committee that we would need to look closely at developing new national economic and social policies, ones which would provide young Canadians, and Canadians in regionally disadvantaged areas, with the knowledge that they would be given the opportunity for full and meaningful employment. Unfortunately that situation has not come to pass under this government and that opportunity, even that concern, does not exist today.
I thank the hon. member who introduced this motion for giving us this brief opportunity to remind the government again that it has basic, fundamental responsibilities, one of which must be the establishment of policies and programs leading to full employment both for the young and for those in regionally disadvantaged areas.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
motion says in a general way that we blame this government for its lack of an industrial strategy making for a planned economy that would give short and particularly long-term results and enable Canadians to enter the labour market and ensure their future.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government has no industrial strategy as such. We run the economy, this country on a day-to-day basis, haphazardly, according to the mood of the moment, nothing more. The problems are faced on an ad hoc basis, but there are no long-term plan aimed at maintaining the employment level, at fighting inflation or preventing those two goals from working against each other. On that score, Mr. Speaker, it is sad to realize it and endure it but it is an actual fact in this country: we have no employment strategy in Canada.
A few years ago, this government announced specific job-creating programs, among others the local initiative programs and opportunities for Youth. In another case, for instance, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was created. Today, in 1976, those local initiative programs have been abolished. For what reason? Monetary restrictions. The same is true of opportunities for Youth.
Mr. Speaker, I am very concerned with that kind of administration not because it comes from the Liberal party but because of that philosophy we have. I am deeply concerned by that. One day, a minister stands up and says to the House: The government has developed a very specific job creation policy; we intend with this strategy to generate a number of job opportunities and for that purpose we invest a few millions. Some time later, the government announces the implementation of another program which is not necessarily related to the previous one, and there we go, as the wind blows.
And finally, because one day the government decided to fight inflation, which it refused to advocate during the election, suddently we have to tighten our belts and forget about creating jobs in Canada or maintaining the rate of employment, since all of a sudden, one fine morning, the government decided that it was important to fight inflation.
Mr. Speaker, the result is, as the motion says, that according to the latest official data of Statistics Canada, the average seasonally adjusted unemployment rate is 7.4 per cent. In Quebec, we hold the record once again, that is 8.3 per cent. Mr. Speaker, as I said previously, I am deeply concerned by this, because with this government we do not know what to expect during the next month, the next three or six months, or the next year. The first point of the motion emphasizes the lack of long-term and short-term planning; it relates this lack of planning, and I agree with this, to the fall in production.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker. First of all, industries themselves, small- and medium-sized businesses in particular, because they do not know what short or long range policies the government will put forward, restrain their investments and their growth, and this is how their employment rate has leveled off so to speak, because of this lack of concern. Second, and it has already been said in this House, our labour legislation, as regards jobs covered by both the federal and provincial codes, our laws and bargaining process are quite outdated, which means once more that small- and medium-sized businesses are the victims of
Industrial Strategy
slow negotiations, inefficient employer-employee dialogue and finally, this is another major reason for the reduction of our per capita gross national product.
I refer once more to the official statistics of the Department of Labour of Canada, which indicate the number of strikes and lock outs in Canada and show again that our bargaining process is not only slow, inefficient, obsolete and outdated but moreover, that it creates in a way endless and very costly disputes between labour and management. Statistics in this regard speak for themselves, Mr. Speaker, and it is not necessary to quote them here.
In this relatively dark picture-and I think this is the actual situation and I am not pessimistic in saying so- there are some elements of hope or spark plugs that come to light at a given time everywhere in Canada. Let us mention in particular the experience of a company named Tricofil, which was completely on the decline, as a result of textile imports, just as it happened in the footwear industry in Canada and in the province of Quebec in particular, where this industry was prevailing. All this happened as a result of government inaction, because of a government strategy which encouraged more imports than any policy designed to support the endeavours of our own industries. We are waking up, Mr. Speaker, with a footwear industry that has disappeared, together with these jobs. In the case of textile, exactly the same type of crisis exists.
Recently, I asked a question of the minister on this subject. He replied that a Canadian textile commission had been established, that many studies are being done on this subject and that we are starting to understand the problem pretty well. No solution has yet been found. We are content to judge dumping cases, but we do not ensure employment protection in our country, and especially in the Eastern Townships, Mr. Speaker, where the problem has taken tremendous proportions.
As an example, I would mention Victoriaville, my own city, where there is an industry called Robin Company and another one called UTEX Company. These plants now operate at only 40 per cent of their production capacity. Why? Because we are unable to face the foreign competition that this government, and I repeat, this government, is importing because of its lack of legislation to protect the Canadian industry and its lack of Canadianism spirit which would make us give first and foremost to Canadians the opportunity to produce themselves the products that we can manufacture locally before importing them.
For political or financial reasons of which I am not aware, the government prefers to encourage imports from countries where the manpower rates are, of course, much lower than ours. This is why the Robin Company, Mr. Speaker, is laying off 200, 300, and 400 people, heads of households, who have been working for 10, 15, 20, 22 or 25 years, who are Canadians like you and me and who can suddenly find themselves in the lower echelons or simply laid off. This is how our whole system of social security in general, especially unemployment insurance, which is a negative program, a disincentive for the worker and because of which we can now say that unemployment competes against work, and this is how you have people with no urge to work or who are discouraged. It is a real drama to lose one's job after 20 years in a factory just because imports are not controlled.

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
When the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) asks for an overall industrial strategy to keep the employment level up, and especially the production level, it means, first, that we are going to impose very strict controls on our importation of products. The same situation prevails in the dairy industry; we import from foreign countries the butter and the cheese that we are able to produce here in Canada. Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that it is because of this particular factor, and many others, that we have overproduction and the government has no other choice but to penalize our own producers. This is some kind of collective discouragement. However, the government is primarily supposed to encourage and support the initiatives of individuals and of businesses.
Mr. Speaker, the consequence is a serious and important loss of jobs which, at the regional or local level, may mean the end to the development of a city or a region or the beginning of that development. This is the case of Victoria-ville with Robin and Utex.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make another remark on this matter. Why did the government abandon the Local Initiatives and Opportunities for Youth Programs? Why? We are told that it is because of monetary cutbacks. So, which reason does the government put forward and how will these programs be replaced? What are we going to do with the students this coming summer? I know that the government will answer that they are going to create 10,000, 15,000 or 20,000 jobs throughout the country. But which industrial strategy does this fit in? Not a political strategy. In which industrial strategy? I fully agree that these programs be abandoned if they do fit into a particular industrial strategy. But this is not the case.
Mr. Speaker, the private sector must be helped rather than hindered. When we meet heads of small and medium industries, they complain of too much administration work to be done to meet government requirements. They tell us this has become extremely complex, and I know this for a fact, because I have gone through that experience personally. Sometimes two, three, or even four full-time professional accountants would be needed, simply to meet the requirements of all government departments such as DREE, Industry, Trade and Commerce, Revenue, and so forth.
What is needed for small and medium businesses is experts, specialists, advisors to help us improve and modernize. Also needed is new labour legislation ensuring efficient negotiations, rather than the kind of legislation that puts us in a confrontation situation from the start.
Work must be encouraged in Canada, rather than unemployment. More stringent and more efficient control of monopolies is needed in the food industry, in the basic materials industry, in the insurance industry or any other field, so that small and medium businesses can breathe and meet genuine competition.
In a number of industries, we face the kind of competition supposedly existing in those supposedly capitalist systems, since there is no genuine competition any more in a number of industries in Canada, because of those pervading monopolies either in the investment property field or

in the money business through chartered banks that create money and are responsible for higher interest rates, or again in the extraction or manufacturing of essential materials.
This is why the cost of living is going up, employment going down, and small and medium firms can no longer compete. We have no anti-monopoly legislation, or if we do have it is collecting dust, as so many other things.
Mr. Speaker, it is one of two things: either we open our ears and work together in support of an employment strategy in Canada, especially for those aged 18 to 35 that are coming into the labour force, who have the necessary skills, who went into debt to complete their studies, and who face nothing else in the immediate future than a service and prolonged period of unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, I think those factors are important. An effort will have to be made above all, once this problem of industrial strategy is recognized, and I think that in that respect the motion of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) is right on, in that the government will have to recognize that the premise of the motion is absolutely true. If it is false the government only has to stand up and say what strategy it intends to draw its inspiration from for the months to come to really restore the confidence of Canadians in their economy.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I will refer to a brochure published not by my political party but by the government of Canada and entitled "Canada 1974", English version, published by Statistics Canada. It was prepared in the Yearbook Division, Statistics Canada. At page 203 of that wonderful brochure one learns extraordinary things. That brochure which is supposed to be given is sold to Canadians so they will know about the policies and how the government of this country works. Those are not general notions that are being transmitted to citizens and particularly immigrants.
So here are the pearls one finds at pages 202, 203 and following concerning the industrial strategy, the creation of employment and the fight against inflation. It will be understood there, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Canada made a choice the day it introduced that anti-inflation legislation. It decided by that legislation to break the process of collective bargaining. Indeed, there is no point in bargaining-you ask for 10 per cent, you get it; you ask for more, it is cut down to 10 per cent, or 12 per cent in certain exceptional cases.
Of course, that does not stop insurance companies from tripling their premiums in one year; nor does it stop the provincial government of Quebec or Ontario from increasing school and municipal taxes at exaggerated and abusive rates but it gives them a mouthful. There is a fight going on against inflation and workers are told: You will limit yourselves to 10 per cent. The whole process of collective bargaining is thus broken. An arbitrary judgment is finally arrived at. So much for that. That is the kind of industrial strategy being offered by the government.
Secondly, the government put an end to programs that were creating temporary employment, such as the Local Initiatives Program and Opportunities for Youth, but at least this meant occasional jobs, it was better than nothing at all. This is abolished. Finally, Mr. Speaker, this same
May 17, 1976

government increases bureaucracy that governs small enterprises and does not do anything against monopolies that stifle small and medium enterprises. I did not invent this, Mr. Speaker, I am referring to this brochure which reads:
The present state of economic knowledge suggests that there would be absolutely no trouble curing unemployment if it were not for the related problem of inflation.
There is the point. I continue to quote:
Unhappily many of the policies designed to increase spending and employment will also tend to exert an upward pressure on prices.
This is the third article on the unemployment inflation pattern.
There is no easy solution to this quandary. There is an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment. Years of significant price increase are years of relatively low unemployment.
I invite my colleagues to read that; it is delightful, Mr. Speaker. The government starts out with the idea it cannot check both unemployment and inflation. There is but one strictly political alternative: fight inflation or fight unemployment. Economists are beginning to suspect-

... I did not say that, Mr. Speaker,...

And the economists who suspect something want to be so specific that they add the following in brackets, and I quote:
(In economic parlance this is referred to as an outward shift in the Phillips curve, which is just another name for the curve or function that shows the trade-off relationship between unemployment and inflation.)
That shows us, Mr. Speaker, how deep we are in obscureness. We live from day to day, which proves once and for all that this government has really no industrial strategy and that it governs from day to day depending on the number of votes it can get. Mr. Speaker, I shall be as brief as possible, considering that my time is over, but the question of the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) is very interesting; it is also very complex. For a long time, on this side, we have stated and maintained that an arbitration policy with a labour court where the employees, the employers and a person totally independent could really lead to a decision on this kind of conflict. And we have always upheld the view that it was about time to have in Canada a permanent collective bargaining system and not one whereby bargaining can take place only when the former agreement, has run out, which means it may take one year for the new contract to be signed.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, granted that one cannot draw many conclusions from one brief answer but what we advocate is a labour court with both parties equally represented and a permanent collective bargaining system. This court could take care of the grievances and problems would be settled as they arise rather than at the end. This is in a way what is now taking place in Quebec. In this manner, Mr. Speaker, solutions would be arrived at or at least the situation would be improved upon.
Right now, it is enough to look at the Quebec public sector where there is no permanent collective bargaining system and where there is not that kind of labour court or compulsory arbitration. You see immediately the kind of mess that province is in. Sick people are not allowed to stay in hospitals, children are kept away from school, teachers cannot teach and all that is proving very expensive.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the solutions I advocate are not ideal. In answering to the question put by the hon. member for Drummond, I will say that these are only elements of solutions, and that if we can devise a lot of technical things today in our society, certainly we can, as intelligent people, find out positive means allowing people to work.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take too much of the time of the House on the motion that is before us today. That does not mean, of course, that what I say succintly will not be right. The motion criticizes the government really in two areas; first of all for its failure to develop an industrial strategy, and then it goes on to point out that this lack of an industrial strategy has resulted in severe problems of location for Canadian workers and industry.
In developing any kind of industrial strategy it is fundamental that you have some control over your economy.

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
This control has to be in two areas in particular, and I want to deal with each separately. First of all, you must have some control over foreign ownership; secondly, and just as important, you must have some control over competing forces within the economy, and this includes both labour and business. Some form of control or consensus or social contract must be arrived at so you can develop an acceptable strategy for the future.
It is getting a little boring to go through a whole litany of figures showing the extent to which Canada is foreign owned, but I still think they bear repeating. For example, 99.9 per cent of the petroleum industry is foreign owned. The figure is 97.7 per cent in the automobile industry, 62 per cent in mining, 83 per cent in the rubber industry, 77 per cent in the electrical apparatus industry, 90 per cent in the computer industry, and 92 per cent in the aircraft and aircraft parts industry. You cannot develop an industrial strategy, or control your own economy, or reduce inequity in society until you get a handle on this major problem of foreign ownership.
If your economy is foreign owned and the country of the parent companies suffer a recession, then workers of subsidiary companies are the first fired and the last hired. The Canadian subsidiary of an American company like Bordens Milk and subsidiaries of any number of other foreign companies are bound to suffer when the parent company decides that it is in the company's best interest to phase out its Canadian operation and thereafter takes the easy route of manufacturing the product at the location of the parent company and shipping it into Canada.
This has happened many times, but one of the examples specified in the motion is Dunlop Tire. The right to manufacture Dunlop tires in Canada is going to be withdrawn by that company. These tires will now be shipped in from the United States, meaning a loss of Canadian jobs and Canadian business. We will have to buy something called the Dayton tire which will compete with the Dunlop tire. Whoever heard of the Dayton tire, and who will find that it can be a successful competitor with a tire that is known and has been patented throughout the world? It is the trademark that has the value as well as the advertising of the name. Because we lack an industrial strategy and a meaningful foreign ownership policy in this country, thousands of Canadian workers are going to be put out of work.
The case of Microsystems is also referred to in the motion. The government allowed a subsidiary of Northern Electric to be closed down after you, Mr. Speaker, I, and the taxpayers of Canada had pumped $40 million into it. This company had developed a very unique and excellent process for building complex microprocessors. There was really no indication that the government knew what that company was doing. As a result, a new Canadian technology that could have been quite successful in world terms went down the tubes.
We will see what are the government's intentions when we examine the Pratt & Whitney situation at Longueuil. Here again the Canadian subsidiary of Pratt & Whitney has a chance to enter into a contract with Rolls Royce to undertake the research, development, and manufacture of a new small jet engine which will be the engine of the 1980's in terms of civil and military jet aviation. It seems that the U.S. justice department found this offensive.

When Pratt & Whitney, a large U.S. aircraft company, locks itself into a contract with Rolls Royce, from an American point of view it looks like a violation of their anti-trust laws. Because of the action of the U.S. justice department, a Canadian subsidiary stands to lose about
1,000	jobs, a large contract for the future and, perhaps just as important, the expertise and talent that go with the aircraft industry.
Canada used to be a world leader in the field of aviation. We pioneered bush piloting and transportation over great areas of this country. We had a lot to show the world. But what has the Liberal government done over the years, Mr. Speaker? It has allowed our aircraft industry to go completely down the tubes. It has allowed all that technology and expertise to go south of the border, leaving us even more as drawers of water and hewers of wood, shipping out our raw materials and our jobs.
