subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I read the motion before us today which says that the government has no industrial strategy, I have the impression that those who introduced it are surely unaware that we now have an industrial strategy.
It is perhaps imperfect or inadequate, according to some members, but I think that those who suggest there is no industrial strategy are insinuating that Canadian history begins with themselves, with the hon. member who introduced this motion. However, I must congratulate the hon. member on this motion which allows us to explain once more all the characteristics of the industrial strategy. During the oral question period or on the adjournment motion some questions were raised which appear again in the motion concerning Westinghouse and Dunlop. I think that the minister answered the questions which were asked but in this debate, it enables us to dwell more at length on the industrial strategy.
Let us first establish the areas of industrial activity and to that end, let me divide it into three sectors. We must first know what we are talking about in order to lay the foundations of an industrial strategy. So, there is the primary sector, which is the resources sector which includes renewable resources. In the primary sector, I would mention renewable resources, and I would also say that in the Western world, among industrial nations, Canada has a unique position in that it is self-sufficient as regards energy and raw materials. The secondary sector is composed of the two following groups of industries: the processing and the manufacturing industries. The tertiary sector is our industries and services sector. Over 50 per cent of jobs in Canada are in that sector, and half of it produces expendable items while the other half includes in about equal proportions personal and public or governmental services. Let us now state the objectives to be sought in planning the future development of our industries.
Then, we must fix the six key goals for the future development of our primary, secondary and tertiary industries. First, we must develop manufacturing and secondary processing industries which would be efficient and competitive at the international level to face the competition in Canada and even outside. Second, we must achieve a situation of full employment in Canadian industry to meet the present and future increase in manpower. Third, we must increase the national revenue and at the same time promote a regional economic expansion which would lessen the disparities between the various regions. Fourth, we must expand the processing of our natural resources in Canada to get the maximum profit out of them. Fifth, we have to establish better control over the Canadian economy and take action so that our future industrial development may be done by Canadians and for Canadians, and I believe that the hon. member who spoke before me men-
Industrial Strategy
tioned the policy on foreign investment, which is one of the priorities. We must contribute to improving the quality of life in Canada, as certain hon. members said today, by reducing the unfavourable effects of industrial activities on our natural environment and social contacts.
Now, without going into the details of those objectives, I would like to mention a few programs which will support these objectives, these key point that I mentioned earlier. We can recognize at least 10 or so major programs which form the heart of the industrial strategy, that is our tax policy, our tarif and trade policy, our industrial support policy, our regional development policy, our labour policy, our competition policy, our foreign investment policy, our mining and energy resource policy, our transportation and communication policy and our environment policy.
I would like to mention a few concrete examples to show to what point it is not a question of developing today an industrial policy and to show to what point we have for several years had a true industrial strategy with specific objective, such as those that I mentioned. If you allow me to do so, I would like to mention certain instruments used to help the industry promote certain products, to expand on the domestic or export markets. I would like to mention also the equipment industry productivity program. We have a new program which allows the Canadian industry to benefit from all types of subsidies, the Industrial Design Assistance Program, which gives financial support aimed at reinforcing the competitives status of Canadian industry.
I will mention the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act, the SPACE Program for the Advancement of Industrial Technology. The department is usually sharing 50 per cent of the costs of new and improved products and commercial processes development projects.
I will also mention the regional development grants. This is presently a very useful program, so necessary as an economic incentive for the areas where the industry would not establish itself. I could also mention the Program for the Advancement of Industrial Technology, whose objective is to help industry-improve its technology, its innovation process, by subsidizing specific products and processes development and improvement projects. And contributions in this case may rise up to 50 per cent of the costs.
I will also mention the Industrial Research Assistance Program, which I have already alluded to. Then there is the Program for Export Market Development. This program has had a large popularity, considering that in 1975, the Export Development Corporation's contribution, through loans, insurance and guarantee, rose up to $2 billion, compared with $1.7 billion for the previous year, that is a 20 per cent increase.
I would like to mention that in respect of foreign investment guarantees, we have recorded a considerable increase. I would like thus to point out that this Export Development Corporation has been quite successful if we consider that in 1975, 40 agreements on loans were signed with foreign borrowers in order to support some Canadian exports. These agreements, including participation by banks, amounted to $1,135 billion which is a record since

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
the creation of the corporation 30 years ago, and an increase of 72 per cent over last year's record of $659 million.
It is, therefore, another tool which can be used to assist industrial expansion. I could mention also another program, CASE, whose purpose is to help the management of small enterprises which often, because of rather rudimentary administrative structures and lack of resources, cannot secure expert services. So there is an assistance program to help small businesses. Some were already mentioned this afternoon. I want to refer to the performance of small businesses last year, in the light of the loans made by the Federal Business Development Bank. But before doing that I would like to say that last year since the CASE program was set up we helped scores of businesses, and over 325 last year.
In the area of assistance loans to small businesses, to which the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) was referring, I will say that if one considers the distribution of loans by provinces, there again the department also has an industrial strategy policy to help small businesses. I note, for example, the votes in effect on September 30, 1975. And in considering the number of businesses that benefitted from loans made by the Federal Business Development Bank-previously the Industrial Development Bank-one notes that in Quebec 4,899 businesses benefitted from loans; in Ontario, 7,255 businesses benefitted from loans; so the relative amounts are $680 million and $861 million which are the votes authorized for the period going from November 1, 1944 to September 30, 1975. There again is a policy, an element of our industrial strategy to help small businesses and make them more efficient.
Reference was made earlier to aeronautics, and I think in that respect I would refer hon. members to the statement by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) about the purchase of Canadair Ltd. from General Dynamics Corporation, of St. Louis, at the cost of $38 million. The minister stated at that time, and I quote:
... that this way there will be excellent possibilities of restructuring the aircraft industry in Canada and getting a stable industry more controlled by Canadians, of developing excellent capabilities in the area of specialized commercial aircraft...
I will also mention the creation of about 3,000 new jobs by 1983. There again, you see that the department is actively looking after the aircraft industry.
I would also like to mention the famous Turnkey Projects. Policies are set up for Turnkey Projects Centres to improve Canadian participation in annual markets estimated at between $20 million and $50 million.
We now have a very good experience in the field of transports, forestry and airports. Here again, we can recognize that last year the Canadian companies have tendered for many Turnkey projects, whose foreign markets are presently estimated at more that $100 million. Before, Canadian bids on such projects were rather rare.
I would also like to mention one of our very interesting experiences in the manufacturing of trains; as far as the contract with the LRC is concerned, these trains are now built at the Bombardier factory in Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere.


I should like to mention the gowth and importance of Canada's consulting and technical service industries in international markets. During the past 10 years the consulting and technical service industries have played an increasingly important role in Canada's international trade activities. It is estimated that this sector of the service industries which contribute more than one billion dollars annually to the Canadian economy consist of some
8,000	firms and export approximately 150 million dollars annually. During the period from 1970 to 1975 their exports have increased approximately 300 per cent. Their impact on Canada's international trade is not only reflected in the services they export but the role they play which leads to the export of manufactured products.
For example, in virtually every case it is the consulting engineer or management consultant which takes the lead in promoting the sale of large capital projects abroad. In 1972 actual Canadian equipment orders for projects on which Canadian consultants were involved totalled $90.3 million. Potential equipment orders were estimated at $343 million.

Mr. Speaker, I think that all these policies have contributed to underline the importance of this aspect and to give the most encouraging results, if we take into account that from 1965 to 1970 we created more than 1,200,000 new jobs, a fact which the minister for Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) mentioned during the debate this afternoon, and if we take into account the number of new jobs created in Canada, about 1,500,000 jobs for the last five years. I think that these figures indicate that Canada has an industrial strategy policy. If we go on implementing this policys, we will contribute to the development of the Canadian economy.
I am very grateful to the hon. member, and I do congratulate him, for proposing this motion which gave us the opportunity to study the present situation, which will help putting new pressures for the development of new measures.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Now we will get the truth.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Now we will get the truth, yes.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) for putting this motion on the Order Paper today. It is certainly a subject that should be talked about although we have already covered it many times already in the question period and in committee. The unemployment figures of today, the disastrous balance sheet, and the global prospects that we foresee, make it imperative that this type of debate should take place.
The key words in the motion are "lack of an industrial strategy", "job losses", "falling production", "uncertainty" and "761,000 Canadians are without jobs". I could not help
May 17, 1976

but feel when listening to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Roy) that he must have used the Canada Year Book to put his remarks together. If we were to take what he said as gospel we would not have so many unemployed people, we would not have the disastrous trade balance; instead we would have a buoyant economy.
I might say at this point, Mr. Speaker, that although the minister is not here tonight he had the courtesy to call and explain that he had a prior engagement, in Vancouver, I believe, and apologized for not being here. I wish to thank him for that courtesy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: No curve?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
What we are really concerned about is the lack of an industrial strategy. We have heard the minister who occupied the portfolio of industry, trade and commerce in the twenty-ninth parliament and the present minister claim that it is impossible to put forth an industrial strategy for Canada. I am sure the present minister has said that at least 15 or 20 times in committee before he changed his tune and said we are developing a sectoral strategy and may have 15 or 20 different strategies for Canada.
We have had eight years of government led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and in that time we have had talking, waffling, programs, studies, seminars, and meetings, but the net result is that we are in the worst trade position we have ever been in; we have the highest interest rates in the western world and the highest mortgage rates in the western world. All we get from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce are alphabet programs and slogans, while the trade deficit grows and the minister forecasts another deficit for next year. We see no strategy, only a retrenchment and a discouraging picture for people involved in industry.
I used to have a great deal of respect for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the people who work there. For years I have defended them and said I thought they were some of the most expert people in government in the western world in regard to trade. When we look at what has happened, however, they must shoulder their share of the blame. They are charged with the responsibility of putting these programs together, although I will admit they have not had very good direction. The former minister of industry, trade and commerce had made a total disaster of the portfolio of science and technology as well; now he is in the energy portfolio and it is in a mess. It seems that they move him in everywhere there is a disaster. As his present department states in its television advertising, if I may paraphrase it, the problem is that he is not part of the solution, he is the problem.
I sometimes wonder what we should do with people in the department who bring forth these programs which fall apart. Perhaps we should hire them on a five-year contract. If they are to be charged with the responsibility of directing industry and the so-called industrial strategy then perhaps you should put them on the same basis as industry. In industry if you do not produce you are out. Maybe that is what we should do here; have these people on a five-year contract and say, "Produce or get out". They
Industrial Strategy
should be charged with the responsibility of bringing forth these programs, but should they have all this security?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems peculiar to me that since it was the New Democratic Party that called for an opposition day today, they should only have one member in the House to support their motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Order, please. Hon. members seem to be concerned as to who is in the House. I do not think that helps the debate; and when hon. members count the members present, that does not help the image of this House. Perhaps hon. members will remember this.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. For the sake of the record-I know the hon. member would not want the record to be incorrect-I point out that three of our members are present. One of them is consulting with one of his colleagues on an important matter. Because he is on the side opposite to me and the hon. member can only see the back of his head, I suggest that the hon. member should see his eye doctor.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also note that three or four committees are meeting this evening and some hon. members who would normally be in the House are attending those committee meetings.
I was talking about the staff of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and saying that perhaps we should put them on the same footing as we put industry. In other words, let us make contracts with them. Then, if they do not produce good programs and implement them properly, we can replace them. In other words, they should either produce or get out. That is the way it is in the business world; perhaps we should explain that to them.
Jobs are created when someone has an idea for a product or service. A person identifies a market. Then he needs money, people, plant, and equipment, to bring the product to the market. He needs the motive of a profit, and confidence that the economy will not fall apart. But he also needs to know that the government is in touch with reality, and is concerned about inflation and foreign trade. And what has happened today?
At present we have 761,000 Canadians unemployed. And what do we hear the government say? We hear the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) making his PR-type announcements to the effect that Canadians do not know their own identity, and so on. Let me tell him that those
761,000	unemployed Canadians know who they are. They are not concerned about the type of identity about which the minister is concerned. They want jobs today; they want pride, something to hold on to; they want to hold their heads up in society and be part of the economic scene.
The young people I have talked to want a job, a home, a car, a cottage in the north-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
And a change of government.

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
They want a change of government. That is right. You know, the final arbiter of this debate will not be the House of Commons; it will be the people of Canada. The 761,000 unemployed are part of the population of Canada and will cast their votes accordingly.
I am about to talk about the government's budgets and the spending estimates, but as the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) has entered the chamber, let me say a few words about a subject which concerns him. We had an interesting debate the other day on science and technology. His department is part of the problem. We heard the parliamentary secretary talking about the development of Canadian industry. He ought to talk to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) about the effects of section 12 of the AIB regulations on research and development. Will the minister do something about that particular section? I hope he will, and I hope he will talk to his colleagues about it because at present it is a disaster.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
If we are concerned about what is happening to our industry we should be concerned about cutbacks in research and development at the university level. Just look at the programs the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has cut back. It has cut back several industrial and research development programs.
The parliamentary secretary spoke at length about the loans the federal business development bank is giving businessmen. Let's not kid ourselves. Those loans are granted at up to 3 per cent above the going rate the banks will charge, if they lend the money. The federal institution is not giving our businessmen any gifts. Look at the Small Business Loans Act and think of the anguish people go through trying to get a loan under the Small Business Loans Act. Then look at the MOSST report on venture capital in Canada. I suggest hon. members should read what it says.
In a few days the government plans to bring down a budget which will look ahead about ten months. You know, other western countries bring down budgets which look two, three, even five years ahead but we are content to look between ten and 12 months ahead.
Profit is the greatest incentive to investment; inflation and uncertainty are the greatest disincentives to investment. We should reflect on that, because when you go out into the real world and talk to people with money to invest you will find that many have put their money in the short-term money market or savings accounts. Why do they not invest it? They have no confidence in the future. There are too many uncertainties, too many year-end philosophizing statements by the Prime Minister on where the "new" economy will go. We must straighten these things out if we are to develop an industrial strategy in this country.
I am particularly annoyed about the attitude of some people who are given responsibility for some industrial programs. Sometimes after a committee meeting I have walked out of the committee room behind some of the departmental people who have attended the meeting, and heard comments made about "snivelling businessmen," those being "snivelling businessmen" who appeared before the committee. I say that attitude is absolutely disgraceful.

The big battle, which will come sooner than later in this country, will be between people who produce taxes and people who consume taxes. Sooner or later those who are operating businesses, working, and paying taxes, and those who are consuming those taxes will meet head on and, let me tell you, it will be one awful battle.
When I consider the government's so-called industrial strategy one of the things that strikes me is what appears to be the complete absence of co-ordination between the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, DREE, and the Department of Finance. Let me put some examples on record.
The Department of Transport has set up a consortium which is to work with the shipping people in Canada to build a series of vessels. The motor vessel Arctic is now under construction at Port Weller. A certain Canadian company submitted a bid on some deck cranes with which the vessel was to be equipped. What happened? They submitted their bid; there were no specifications. After they had put their bid in they told the shipping people that the cranes were of 85 per cent Canadian content. The people who make the decisions in Canada Steamship Lines said to them, "Don't mention Canadian content; that will be a mark against you." The crane people said, "Our cranes are of 85 per cent Canadian content." The shipping people said, "Don't mention that."
And what happened? The government people ended up giving the order to a company in Norway. Ten of these vessels are to be built, and all sorts of merchant vessels are being built in the United States which will use this equipment. The Canadian company developed a market for its product. Although this was an opportunity to introduce a new product which had never before been manufactured in Canada to the Canadian scene, despite the fact that there was a chance to get in on the ground floor, the order was given to a company in Norway.
When the people I talked to looked into this matter, they were flabbergasted, astounded. They were told that the company in Norway will supply a crane using low pressure hydraulics, because that is necessary. That, I submit, was a bunch of garbage. My own company just finished a series of tests on some cranes mounted on crawler tractors which are to be used in the high Arctic. The particular crane in question was chosen because it uses a high pressure hydraulics system, which, in our cold weather tests and in our cold weather environment, is much more efficient than a low pressure system.
That is the only reason they gave. Price was not a factor. It was not a case of low bid or anything else. The prices were relatively close. There was no specification whatsoever.
There is a case of a small manufacturer in my area. He makes, of all things, clay pigeons. Some hon. members may have read about this recently in the paper. There are 35 million clay pigeons consumed in Canada yearly. Searle Industries manufactures 25 million of these. The balance is made in British Columbia, and by another small company in Hamilton. The industry is actually in a position today of oversupply. This person has approximately 10 million clay pigeons in stock.
May 17, 1976

What do you think has happened? The Department of Regional Economic Expansion gave a $65,000 grant to a company from France which is going to put up a clay pigeon manufacturing plant in Quebec. Here we have a company in Hamilton whose employees are on half time, or unemployed and drawing unemployment insurance, and we will now have a new plant that is going to supply a market that is already in an oversupply situation. What sort of nonsense is that?
When we talked to the regional people at DREE, they said that seven new gun clubs are starting up and that will look after this industry. That is a lot of nonsense. With the automated plant now in operation, they can turn out these clay pigeons.
For the Olympics they will not be using clay pigeons made in Canada. They will be imported from France, even though this man has ten million in inventory. How ridiculous can we get!
There is no coordination between DREE, Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the Department of Finance. We have had on-again off-again capital cost allowances. Where does that leave us? I wonder whether some of the people in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce have ever had anything to do with business or whether they simply came out of the academic world into government and decided to tell how everything is to be done.
When you are planning and developing a business, time is a very important factor. It takes time to develop a market, time to develop sources of capital, and time to train people. What our business people really need is a development policy that will give them time. They need a span of years in order to put together the various ingredients that make up a business.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret having to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening to interventions by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) it seemed as though they were looking so closely at the trees they lost their capacity to see the forest. One wonders where they have been for the past 30 years. When preparing their speeches they did not look at what has happened in the past 30 years.
In the past 30 years there has been a rapid increase in our industrial growth. We have developed a strong steel industry, as well as pulp and paper, chemical, oil and gas, plastics, synthetic fibre, plate glass, aluminum, electronics, to mention just a few. We are now manufacturing different types of heavy industrial equipment as well as a very wide range of consumer and durable goods which we export.
Today manufactured goods account for 40 per cent of our total exports as compared to about 10 per cent 20 years ago. As for minerals, we are now processing and refining more of these here in Canada before exporting them. For instance, in the past we used to export raw iron ore; now we process this into iron ore pellets. The same applies to copper and nickel, as well as forest products.
Canada participated in the Kennedy Round of negotiations to remove tariff barriers to world trade in progressive
Industrial Strategy
stages. Canada depends on exports and it is to our advantage to have world markets open to us.
We signed the auto pact with the United States to ensure that more of the manufacturing of the cars we buy is done in Canada. This pact has resulted in the growth of our auto parts industry. The pact accounts for a significant portion of our finished exports.
We modernized our ports and went in for container shipping to maximize the advantages of our St. Lawrence Seaway. We are now manufacturing 2,000 new rail cars to transport our wheat and other bulk export products. We established Panarctic to own outright the major share of any future development of our northern resources. We established the CRTC which has resulted in the growth of a Canadian radio and television program industry. We now rank third in the world in the production of musical records. Our government has considerably increased the amounts of money available as loans to small companies, as well as the grants for research.
We formulated a foreign policy clearly aimed at expanding the scope of our export markets. We signed trade agreements with the Soviet Union and the People's Republic of China which led to huge sales of grain. Because of our bilingual character we not only have an affiliation with the British Commonwealth countries but we have an affiliation with the French-speaking nations of the world. During the past few years our trade with the Francophone nations almost doubled, and in the future we can look . forward to a steady growth in these markets.
We established the Export Development Corporation in 1969. This was very well described by the parliamentary secretary. This was done to put an emphasis on exports. It is essential because Canada depends on exports to maintain our high standard of living and our jobs.
We established the Canada Development Corporation, described earlier by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), to finance new Canadian industries and buy shares in existing Canadian companies that are expanding. As recently as last week there was a report that the United States government was about to place an order with Bombardier for highly industrialized products in the amount of $36 million. This is possible because of the technology and know-how developed in Canada over the years.
There are two other areas, perhaps of lesser importance, but significant for cultural and aesthetic reasons. We have done extremely well in the field of developing Canadian fashions and the sale of Canadian books, particularly in Europe.
There are areas in which we have to improve our performance, making sure that we keep up with changing technology and the very keen and competitive production in other nations. However, it seems to me we have laid a sound base for our present and future growth.
We do have to deal with the difficulties which are characteristic of the seventies, of course. First, we have to keep in mind that automation is replacing manpower at a faster rate than in past decades; we must therefore intensify our efforts to retrain workers as some industries become obsolete and others offer new opportunities. Then again we

May 17, 1976
Industrial Strategy
have to take into account the existence of stiffer competition for export markets. We must also give thoughtful consideration to the rapid depletion of our environmental resources.
I notice that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) is to speak next. I know that in his usual way he will make a learned and well-documented speech based upon the facts and upon solid information. If he does this, I am sure he will be bound to reach the conclusion that the Government of Canada has done well for the nation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for indicating I might do some of those things, but I am afraid I shall have to disappoint him.
I am surprised that so little has been said in this debate by other government spokesmen or the official opposition about their attitude toward an industrial strategy for Canada. One of the things for which the New Democratic Party took some credit in the last parliament was the development of a review board to assess foreign takeovers. We, in that minority parliament, were proud of our contribution to this policy; we thought that an industrial strategy would develop as a consequence-a strategy of making sure that if any further foreign industry were allowed into Canada the industry concerned would be serving a purpose of value to the Canadian people. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the government, as has been the case so often in the past, took a very good idea and failed to follow through. The intention was to enable the Canadian public to have the benefit, whenever possible, of the gains which could be expected by allowing certain American companies to enter this country.
We might have used this system to make sure that U.S. companies coming to Canada did something for Canadians for a change, rather than for themselves. We might have made it possible for Canadian citizens to participate in the ownership of those companies. But what has happened? There have been no reports forthcoming as to the concessions Canada has made when allowing U.S. take-overs. My hon. friends have documented cases involving Dunlop, Firestone, White Industries, and a number of other companies to show that once again we have sold out the Canadian public for the sake of the introduction of U.S. capital into this country and the experience which may flow from it. But, Mr. Speaker, such industry is always used for the benefit of Americans; it seldom does much more than provide menial jobs at the lower end of the activity in Canada.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I heard a number of hon. members deploring the worsening in our relationship between industry and labour and consequent loss of production through work stoppages. Some of them referred to the number of days which had been lost as a result of strikes. They referred sadly to the fact that we may have lost 10 million man-hours in strikes last year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Eleven million man-hours.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO INSTITUTE INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
I stand corrected. And because of this, certain members of the House would scrap the whole of our procedures in the field of labour relations, the whole of the grievance procedure, everything we have built up in this

area over the years. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that those who complained so bitterly about the loss of those manhours were weeping crocodile tears. Nobody who has any brains in this House really believes that those 11 million lost hours matter a damn.
Let me draw attention to the fact that at the present time 7 per cent of our population is unemployed. In numerical terms this amounts to some 750,000, and some of them have been unemployed for years. Two thousand hours make up an industrial man year. If we multiply 2,000 man-hours by 750,000 we come up with a figure of 1,500 billion. That is the number of man-hours we have lost over a year because of unemployment. Those who weep crocodile tears over the 11 million man-hours lost through strikes forget about the other 1,489,000,000 which have been lost because of unemployment.
It is a sad thing for this country to find itself controlled by a government which has for years suffered from a C. D. Howe philosophy. His philosophy was to engineer a deal, engineer any deal which would cause a flow one way or the other-it didn't matter as long as there was a flow. But the flow has almost invariably been in the wrong direction. It is true we have expanded our steel industry, it is true we have increased the scale of our manufacturing. Which country in the world has not? Italy, which is almost bankrupt, has done so. And so has England. We sure as hell do not want to get into that group just because we want to put our achievements in a good light. Just think how much better off we could be, how much richer we could be, if we could use those 1,500 billion man-hours lost through unemployment, if we could find gainful occupations for these people.
We have heard talk about the fight that will take place between those who are paying taxes and those who are receiving the benefits of those taxes. I hear statements also that unemployment insurance is being abused. It is being abused. It is being abused by the government mainly. It is being abused by a large section of industry which is operated at 60 per cent capacity; it is also being abused by a very few people who are recipients of it. But I know that most of the people who are receiving unemployment benefits and who come to my office are anxious to get a job; if a job were available they would prefer to take it. But no job is made available.
Anyone who considers the regional transportation arrangements made in this country must wonder what has happened to national industrial strategy. We have continued to bring people to the cities rather than take jobs to the people.
Members on the other side have referred to trade missions. I have talked to many people who have travelled across the world representing Canada on trade missions and they are not proud of our trade representatives ove-reas. Our trade people do not know whom they should talk to in the various business fields. Our ambassadors are eunuchs when it comes to developing trade and assisting our representatives travelling abroad. Let us start using the good people that we have.
Tomorrow we are going to make one of the most stupid expenditures we have ever made, Mr. Speaker. We are
May 17, 1976

probably going to tell Lockheed in the United States that we will back the U.S. government if the U.S. government will back Lockheed in building us 18 Orion aircraft. Why do we want these aircraft? It is for military prestige. They are prestige aircraft. These aircraft are not worth a damn when it comes to saving sailors lost at sea or for supervising our 200 mile coastal limit. And let us not forget that we have the longest coastline in the world. What is more, Mr. Speaker, I am sure we do not have enough fuel to fly these aircraft at 500 or 600 miles an hour at 40,000 or 50,000 feet along our coastline. This operation can be done by satellite and it will not require the expenditure of any money.
We once had the potential in this country to build one of the best aircraft ever made. I have had some experience of the aircraft industry over a number of years, both in the air force and in aircraft factories, including those in Montreal and Toronto. It is my opinion that when we built the Arrow the mistake was not in the building of it; the mistake was made by the government of the day in that it did not blackmail all the other NATO countries, as they do us, into placing orders for the aircraft. We could not get any orders for the aircraft and so we could not make up our mind whether it should be a light bomber, a fighter aircraft, or what. As a result we built a kind of utility plane that required so much equipment to fly it that we could not fly it very far.
That plane was way ahead of its time and, in my opinion, the Arrow could still out-compete most of the aircraft in the world today. The trouble was that we did not have the ability to sell it. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we had no industrial strategy.
The government never made one sale of that aircraft. It built the damned plane but did not know what to do with it, so the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), because he did not like the president of the company, cut it up with a torch. I do not think there is one left in Canada today to give an indication of our former potential and in the aeronautical field.
Certainly we do not need the Orion. With 18 Orion aircraft we are not going to save Europe. Neither are we going to supervise our 200 mile coastal limit. However, with the technology we have in Canada we can still build aircraft. We could build an aircraft along the lines of the Otter and the Lear jet that we are going to build for Mr. Lear. This would be a plane that would meet our requirements and leave us with some money to build ships and equipment to save sailors lost off our coasts, fishermen who are in dire need of protection and have not been getting it.
I am surprised that government members should only speak of what they have accomplished. In these days of austerity, which is more apparent outside than inside the House, I am sure the government is planning things it would like to accomplish if it had the wherewithal. I am equally sure the government is considering developing further our industrial potential. However, we cannot compete with a highly industrialized country like the United States. How in the hell do we think we will ever get into that market?

subtopic: ENERGY-STUDY OF FUNDY TIDAL POWER-DATE OF COMMENCEMENT
ENERGY-STUDY OF FUNDY TIDAL POWER-DATE OF COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 28, 1974, the then minister of energy, mines and resources, our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), issued a joint statement with the premiers of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia announcing that a study program would be undertaken to review, update, and extend the Atlantic tidal power programming board's report released in October, 1969, entitled "Feasibility of Tidal Power Development in the Bay of Fundy".
Despite repeated requests from my colleagues and myself it was not until March of this year, 16 months later, that the initiation of this study was announced. On June 2 of last year the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Foster) told me, as recorded at page 6370 of Hansard, that federal and provincial officials would meet within a week to "allocate specific study work projects and arrange for their execution". Yet it was not until nine months later that the study was announced. The federal government has been dragging its heels on the matter of Fundy tidal power.
When the announcement was made in the press release, the first phase of studies was announced and they were very accurately identified. On page 4 of the news release, in the first paragraph we find the following:
Other aspects of the first phase studies include consideration of socio-economic and environmental aspects which will be carried out concurrently with the foregoing major task studies. These aspects are now in the process of being defined and it is anticipated study contracts will be arranged shortly.
That was two months ago today.
As a result of this shortsightedness by the government, we in the Atlantic region find ourselves facing staggering energy costs. It is not my intention to repeat earlier speeches I have made pointing out the advantages Fundy power would have energywise and industrially, not just for the Atlantic region but for the entire country.
It is also my hope that the gravity of the situation is well understood by the government following the recent debate on energy in the Atlantic provinces. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) summed up my feelings so ably that day by stating that Canada does not prosper unless all of Canada prospers.
Maritimers cannot help but note the contrast between the alacrity with which the federal government has leaped into an investment of $300 million, or more, in the Syncrude project in Alberta and the indifference it displays to tidal power development possibilities of the Bay of Fundy. The two situations have much in common. In a world increasingly conscious of an impending energy shortage,

both represent the possible development of very large quantities of energy now lying dormant. The difference is that the Alberta tar sands, vast though their extent may be, contain a fossil fuel as their active ingredient. Like conventional oil wells or coal deposits, they are subject to depletion and eventual exhaustion. The Fundy tides, on the contrary, represent a permanent source of energy which, barring a global catastrophe, are as likely to be as productive a million years from now as they could be today.
There are other differences, of course. Fundy is located in a region of Canada to which Ottawa's traditional attitude is one of indifference. We are not opposed to getting all the oil we can from the tar sands of Alberta. We have seen some ominous forecasts of serious energy shortages rushing upon the world. Canada is blessed with abundant energy sources of a number of kinds. We would be in default if we neglected to utilize any of them, whether tar of tides. We should get busy on both.
Had Fundy proceeded in the late 1960's it would be well under way by now. Costs rise every day as money loses purchasing power every day. The price of Fundy in 1969, far from being expensive, was cheap relative to the price of Fundy in 1976.
Ineptitude, wedded to confusion and knee-deep in indecision and procrastination, mark this program like so many others that are essential to the region and national purpose. There are people in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and DREE who are capable, willing, and who desire to get on with the assigned task. Surely it is time that the people who can and will do the job were allowed to get on with it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-STUDY OF FUNDY TIDAL POWER-DATE OF COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to respond to the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie).
The joint federal-provincial feasibility study on the development of tidal power in the Bay of Fundy commenced during this past year. The study is being carried out under the direction of a federal-provincial management committee in accordance with an agreement between the Government of Canada and the governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
The management committee awarded contracts involving nine major engineering consulting firms in specific task areas relating to the design of tidal power plants, optimization of tidal power schemes, and the marketing and transmission of tidal power in accessible marketing areas.
In addition, arrangements have been made with the ocean and aquatic sciences branch of the federal Department of the Environment to acquire special data relative to the tidal phenomenon in the Bay of Fundy and to develop a mathematical model to analyse the effects that one or more major tidal power developments in the Bay of Fundy would have on the tidal regime.
Contractual arrangements are also being developed to carry out preliminary studies on socio-economic and environmental aspects of developing tidal power in the Bay of Fundy area.
May 17, 1976

It is expected that the phase I element of the current study will be completed in the early months of 1977.
I understand that the first stage will be completed early this summer and the second stage will then be carried out during the later half of 1976.
Since tidal power is primarily an energy-oriented matter it is appropriate that the federal responsibility for the current joint study program remain with the federal Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
In regard to physical presence in the area, it is pointed out that both the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are represented in all aspects of the study as well as the over-all review board by senior personnel from the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission and the Nova Scotia Power Corporation. Hence there is every opportunity for input of local knowledge and provincial considerations in respect to both electrical energy supply and industrial development considerations on this most important project.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-COW-CALF STABILIZATION PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ALBERTA PROPOSAL-POSSIBLE DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION
AGRICULTURE-COW-CALF STABILIZATION PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ALBERTA PROPOSAL-POSSIBLE DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question with which I wish to deal arises out of one of the series of questions which I have posed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) over the last six to eight months. This one was specifically put on January 30. The questions were put in an attempt to badger the minister into doing something for the very hard pressed cow-calf sector of the beef industry, to do something, I might add, which the minister had promised not only on his political haymaking excursions into western Canada but indeed here in the House of Commons and to the press.
The question I posed on January 30, as recorded at 10480 of Hansard, was as follows:
Can the minister advise the House whether a federal-provincial cow-calf stabilization program is being developed and whether any progress has been made in efforts to shore-up this badly shaken industry?
The minister replied that he was still having discussions. He stated:
A program will start on January 1, 1976 and terminate at the end of December, 1976, covering the calendar year for beef in Canada.
It is now the end of May, going into June. We have no beef stabilization program and it appears obvious that the cow-calf producers can expect absolutely nothing-zilch. Quite frankly, the period in which any aid or assistance could be given to them is pretty well passed inasmuch as the serious impact on the cow-calf industry was in the fall and in early winter.
The minister has viewed every conceivable ploy imaginable to blame for his failure to come through and fulfill his commitment. He has blamed the Canadian cattlemen, the stock growers, and the provinces, but he himself has not accepted any blame or responsibility. We know that the intervention by the federal government in bringing forth a beef policy which varied around 29 or 30 times over a period of 18 months had a lot to do and contributed immeasurably to the plight of beef producers, but particularly the cow-calf producer.
Adjournment Debate
All we had in terms of support for the cow-calf industry were empty promises. The actions of the minister in this regard constitute a litany of broken promises.
We started with the Agricultural Stabilization Act, which we debated in this House about a year ago. It was given Royal Assent on July 31. It was heralded as a major advance in national farm policy. What did this do for the cow-calf industry? It did absolutely nothing, but there was much hot air from the minister's mouth. On September 19 an article by Armin Hecht in the Edmonton Journal read in part as follows:
A federal cow-calf stabilization program will be announced in two weeks at the earliest, federal Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan's office said Thursday.
The plan will be similar to the federal government's stabilization plan for fat cattle.
Officials in Mr Whelan's department are working feverishly at the program, a spokesman in the minister's office said. Things are complicated because it will be the first time two separate plans will cover the same commodity.
This kind of fever only produced convulsions from the minister, as far as I am concerned. The article went on to
say:
Officials in Mr. Whelan's office said if there is anyone who can make a cow-calf subsidy program workable, it will be Mr. Whelan.
The minister is fully aware of the depressed state of the industry and is concerned that the plan is not yet in operation, his office said.
His concern can only be categorized as much less than genuine.
On December 20, 1975, again quoting from the Edmonton
Journal-.
Alberta Agriculture Minister Marvin Moore is optimistic that long bogged-down talks to create a cow-calf income stabilization program may soon result in success.
After meeting with federal Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan and his provincial counterparts, Mr. Moore said he expects an early decision by Ottawa on a proposal to salvage the badly shaken industry.
It went on to say:
A cow-calf assistance program would be available very quickly-if it were up to federal Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan.
He is very happy with the Alberta proposal, provincial Agriculture Minister Marvin Moore said Friday.
It has been the same old litany of broken promises.
Then on January 29 a headline in the Edmonton Journal read, "Aid for cow-calf operators 'slim' ", The article stated in part:
Chances that Ottawa will still come up with a cow-calf support program are pretty slim, a source in federal Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan's office has indicated.
So there we have it. We can only gather from those statements in the press that if the minister ever had any clout in the cabinet he has lost it. It is obvious he cannot convince his cabinet colleagues to come forth and assist in shoring up a badly shaken industry, and I do not know why the minister has not come clean and told the producers of this country that he cannot do anything for them, rather than beating around the bush with this political garble. The minister is, and has been guilty of misleading the cow-calf producers of this country into believing that something was going to be done while he knew all along
9SS68-27

Adjournment Debate
that nothing could be done. He searched for excuses. His answers in the House have been evasive and flippant, almost to the point of being devious at some times.
In the end the minister has betrayed the cow-calf producers, and he should be and shall be reminded of this at every opportunity. He has not acted in good faith with the producers. He has failed to accept his rightful responsibility and obligation to the cow-calf producers, and from here on we will have suspicions about the minister's motives.

speechtext:
The Agricultural Stabilization Act names cattle as one of the named commodities. Cattle, of course, was a named commodity in the original stablization act, and this was not changed in the amendments last year. As the House knows, the minimum mandatory support for named commodities under the amended act is 90 per cent of the average price of the last five years adjusted for changes in production costs in the current year as compared with the average production costs of the last five years. Ever since the original 1958 legislation "cattle" has been interpreted to mean slaughter cattle. We continue to consider that the named commodity, cattle, is represented by slaughter cattle. The same principle is applied to hogs and to sheep with the named commodity being market hogs and market lambs.
There has, of course, been considerable discussion about the desirability of having a stabilization program for the cow-calf sector of the beef industry. Some of the provinces
have implemented such programs. As I have indicated on earlier occasions, we have also considered providing support for this sector as a designated commodity under the act. This is a complex issue because of the nature of the industry, the conflicting views of cow-calf producers as to the desirability of having a program, and due to the fact that some provinces now have individual programs.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few words to the official answer of the department and respond to some of the hon. member's allegations which I think are absolutely inconceivable. The Progressive Conservative members are the first to say that if we want to carry out a national program, we must consult. When we do so and they do not agree, we must reach a consensus; it takes time and if we acted unilaterally, they would be the first ones to complain about it. The hon. member referred to a few articles in the Edmonton Journal in which the minister is quoted as saying he is ready to develop a cow-calf program. Of course, the minister is ready. Now, are the provinces ready as well? Alberta wants one thing. Quebec, British Columbia want something else, Ontario wants yet another thing. They must come to an agreement. If we are to develop a national program, all provinces must be in agreement.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the answer is very simple. This program, after some discussion, is still at the experimental stage, there are some problems with a few provinces at present but as soon as they are solved, the government will carry out a national program that will satisfy all provinces.
